course.title: Data Structures and Algorithms
course.description: Learn how the standard containers work, what they cost, and how to pick one, from arrays and hash tables to heaps, graphs and dynamic programming, with every claim counted by hand and checked in Python.
course.audience: Someone who finished How Computers Solve Problems or has equivalent footing: they know steps, branches, loops, linear and binary search, and the idea that cost grows with input size. They can read and write short Python functions. Mathematics beyond arithmetic and a little algebra is not needed.

paragraphs: Every program that handles more than a handful of items has to decide how to hold them, and each choice makes some operations cheap and others dear. An array reads any element at once but moves its neighbours when one is inserted, a linked list does the reverse, and a hash table finds an item by its key at the price of spare room for collisions. A data structure is one such arrangement of items together with the operations it offers, and an algorithm is a procedure that works on it, such as sorting its items or searching it for a route.

The subject can look like a catalogue of names to memorise, yet nearly every claim in it can be settled by counting. Counting the elements that move when one is inserted at the front of an array gives the price of that operation, counting the copies that a growing array makes shows that appending stays cheap on average, and counting the vertices and edges that a search visits shows how long it will take on a network of any size. A count of this kind states how the cost grows with the size of the input on any machine, which lets you compare two designs before writing either of them and choose a container from the operations a problem needs.
The programs are short Python functions, and the course assumes you have met steps, branches, loops and binary search in How Computers Solve Problems.
outcomes: You'll be able to count the steps of nested loops and state their growth class.
You'll be able to say what arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, trees and heaps cost for their main operations.
You'll be able to trace insertion sort, merge sort and quicksort by hand.
You'll be able to run breadth-first search, depth-first search and Dijkstra's algorithm on a small graph.
You'll be able to turn a recursive problem into a table and see when greedy choices fail.
You'll be able to choose a container from the operations a problem needs.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on How Computers Solve Problems.

modules.title: Cost and containers
modules.description: Count what code does, then meet the basic ways of holding a sequence: arrays, growing arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues.

modules.title: Lookup and order
modules.description: Find items by key with hashing, use recursion, and put items in order with merge sort and quicksort.

modules.title: Trees, graphs and reuse
modules.description: Organise items in trees and heaps, explore graphs, find cheapest paths, and avoid repeated work.

concepts.title: Step count
concepts.summary: The step count T(n) is the number of times a chosen basic operation executes for an input of size n.

concepts.title: Big-O bound
concepts.summary: f(n) is O(g(n)) when, beyond some n, f(n) stays below a constant multiple of g(n).

concepts.title: Triangular count
concepts.summary: A loop whose inner bound grows by one each pass runs 0 + 1 + ... + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2 times, which is quadratic.

concepts.title: Array
concepts.summary: An array stores equal-sized elements in consecutive memory, so element i sits at base + i x size.

concepts.title: Constant-time indexing
concepts.summary: Because the address is arithmetic, reading or writing a[i] costs the same for any i.

concepts.title: Shifting
concepts.summary: Inserting or deleting in the middle of an array moves every element after that position by one slot.

concepts.title: Capacity and size
concepts.summary: A dynamic array keeps a size (items stored) and a capacity (slots reserved), and appends are free while size < capacity.

concepts.title: Doubling
concepts.summary: When full, the array allocates twice the capacity and copies every element once, which makes the total copying for n appends less than 2n.

concepts.title: Amortised cost
concepts.summary: Amortised cost is the total cost of a sequence of operations divided by their number, which can be low even when a single operation is expensive.

concepts.title: Node
concepts.summary: A node holds a value and a reference to the next node, and the list is the chain from a head reference.

concepts.title: Insertion by rerouting
concepts.summary: Inserting after a known node changes two references and moves nothing, so it costs constant time.

concepts.title: Sequential access
concepts.summary: Reaching the k-th node means following k references from the head, which costs O(k).

concepts.title: Stack
concepts.summary: A stack allows adding and removing only at one end, so the last item added is the first removed (LIFO).

concepts.title: Queue
concepts.summary: A queue adds at the back and removes from the front, so the first item added is the first removed (FIFO).

concepts.title: Double-ended queue
concepts.summary: A deque supports constant-time adds and removes at both ends, which is why it is used for queues in Python rather than list.pop(0).

concepts.title: Hash function
concepts.summary: A hash function maps a key to an integer, and taking it modulo the table size gives a bucket index.

concepts.title: Collision
concepts.summary: Two keys that land in the same bucket collide, and a table must resolve this by chaining entries in a bucket or probing for a nearby free slot.

concepts.title: Load factor
concepts.summary: The load factor is stored entries divided by buckets, and expected lookup cost grows with it, so tables resize when it passes a threshold.

concepts.title: Base case
concepts.summary: A recursive function needs a case that returns without calling itself, or it never stops.

concepts.title: Call stack
concepts.summary: Each active call keeps its own variables on a stack, and returning resumes the caller at the line after the call.

concepts.title: Call count recurrence
concepts.summary: For fib, calls(n) = 1 + calls(n-1) + calls(n-2), which grows exponentially because the same subproblems are recomputed.

concepts.title: Inversion
concepts.summary: An inversion is a pair of positions i < j with a[i] > a[j], and insertion sort performs exactly one shift per inversion.

concepts.title: Merge
concepts.summary: Merging two sorted lists repeatedly takes the smaller front item, producing a sorted list in at most len(a) + len(b) - 1 comparisons.

concepts.title: Divide and conquer
concepts.summary: Merge sort splits the list in halves, sorts each recursively and merges, giving log2 n levels each doing about n work.

concepts.title: Partition
concepts.summary: Partitioning rearranges a list around a pivot so everything not greater than the pivot lies before it and everything greater lies after it, fixing the pivot's final position.

concepts.title: Worst case
concepts.summary: Quicksort with a last-element pivot on already sorted input splits n into 0 and n-1 each time, making n(n-1)/2 comparisons.

concepts.title: Comparison lower bound
concepts.summary: Any comparison sort must distinguish n! orderings with yes/no answers, so it needs at least ceil(log2(n!)) comparisons in the worst case.

concepts.title: Search-tree property
concepts.summary: In a binary search tree every key in a node's left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger.

concepts.title: Traversal
concepts.summary: In-order traversal visits left subtree, node, right subtree and so lists the keys in sorted order; pre-order and post-order visit the node first and last.

concepts.title: Height
concepts.summary: Search, insert and delete follow one root-to-leaf path, so they cost O(h), which is log n when balanced and n when the tree is a chain.

concepts.title: Heap property
concepts.summary: In a min-heap every node is no larger than its children, so the smallest item is at the root.

concepts.title: Heap in an array
concepts.summary: A complete binary tree fits in an array where the children of index i are 2i+1 and 2i+2 and the parent of i is (i-1)//2.

concepts.title: Priority queue
concepts.summary: A priority queue removes the item with the highest priority first, and a heap does insert and remove in O(log n).

concepts.title: Graph
concepts.summary: A graph is a set of vertices and a set of edges between pairs of them, stored for a program as adjacency lists mapping each vertex to its neighbours.

concepts.title: Breadth-first search
concepts.summary: BFS explores vertices in order of distance from the start by using a queue, so the first time it reaches a vertex is by a path with the fewest edges.

concepts.title: Depth-first search
concepts.summary: DFS follows one path as far as it can before backing up, using recursion or an explicit stack.

concepts.title: Weighted graph
concepts.summary: In a weighted graph each edge has a cost, and a path's cost is the sum of its edge costs.

concepts.title: Relaxation
concepts.summary: Relaxing an edge u to v replaces the best known distance to v with dist[u] + w when that is smaller.

concepts.title: Dijkstra's algorithm
concepts.summary: Dijkstra repeatedly finalises the unfinalised vertex with the smallest known distance, which is correct when all weights are non-negative.

concepts.title: Overlapping subproblems
concepts.summary: A problem has overlapping subproblems when the same smaller question is asked many times, so storing answers saves work.

concepts.title: Recurrence and table
concepts.summary: A dynamic program defines each answer from smaller ones and fills a table in an order that guarantees those smaller answers exist.

concepts.title: Greedy failure
concepts.summary: Taking the largest coin first is not always optimal: with coins 1, 3 and 4, making 6 greedily uses three coins while 3 + 3 uses two.

lessons.title: Counting steps in nested loops

blocks.text: Here are two loops that differ in a single bound. In `for i in range(8): for j in range(8):` the line inside runs 64 times, whereas changing the inner bound to `range(i)` makes it run only 28 times.
Counting how often a line runs is how the cost of a program is stated before the program is run, and every container and algorithm after this one is judged by it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count how often the inside of nested loops runs, write the count as a formula in n, and name its growth class.
intro.whyItMatters: The cost of every container and algorithm in this course is stated as a step count and a growth class.

recap.keyIdea: The step count of nested loops comes from multiplying the bounds of loops inside one another and adding the counts of blocks in sequence, and its growth class keeps only the fastest-growing term without its constant.

blocks.text: You counted the runs of an inner line as a formula in n, which for a loop whose inner bound is the outer variable gave the triangular count n(n − 1)/2. Dropping constant factors and slower terms then put that count in the class O(n²), the same class as a full n by n grid, and put a loop with a fixed inner bound of 3 in the class O(n).

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the simplest container, the array, and counts the elements that have to move when something is inserted into it.

lessons.orientation: Count how many times the innermost statement of nested loops runs, write the count as a formula in n, and name its growth class.
lessons.nextAction: Work out where an array element lives from its index, and count how many elements move when you insert into an array.

lead.text: A program does not take a fixed amount of work, because the work depends on how much data it is given. To measure it we pick one statement inside the loops, the line that does the repeated job, and count how many times it runs. Given n values, it would run n times, and this number of runs, written as a function of the input size n, is called the **step count** T(n).
Here T(n) = n, so step through the trace and watch `x` rise by one on every pass of the loop.

afterFigure.text: Which statement to count is a choice, and any statement that runs once per pass will do, provided you keep to it for the whole analysis.

reveal.text: The inner loop restarts on every outer pass, which is the fact the next screen turns into a rule.

lead.text: Each pass of the outer loop starts the inner loop afresh, so the inner loop's passes are repeated once per outer pass, and the line ran 5 × 3 = 15 times.

Replace the outer bound by n and keep the inner bound at 3, and the count is 3n. That is a multiple of n, so the work grows in step with n, exactly as it does for a single loop. Only when both bounds are n is the count n × n = **n²**.

afterFigure.text: Two loops therefore do not in themselves mean n². An inner loop of 3 passes costs three times the work of a single loop, and doubling n doubles the count, whereas in the n-by-n arrangement doubling n makes the count *four* times larger, because both the rows and the columns have doubled.

diagram.caption: One cell for each run of the inner line, one row for each pass of the outer loop. Use the buttons to change the inner bound.

lead.text: In the loop `for i in range(n): for j in range(i):` the inner bound is `i`, which changes from one outer pass to the next. The pass with i = 0 runs the inner line no times, the pass with i = 1 runs it once, and the last pass, with i = n − 1, runs it n − 1 times. The total is therefore 0 + 1 + 2 + ... + (n − 1), and the shaded cells in the figure form a staircase, a pattern called a **triangular count**.

afterFigure.text: To add this up without writing out every term, write the sum twice, the second copy in reverse order, and add the copies column by column. The first column adds 0 and n − 1, the second adds 1 and n − 2, and every one of the n columns adds to n − 1, so the two copies together make n(n − 1). The sum itself is half of that, **n(n − 1)/2**, and for n = 8 it gives 8 × 7 ÷ 2 = 28, the number of shaded cells you see when the figure is set to n = 8.

steps.headline: Count the runs of count = count + 1 in: for i in range(6): for j in range(i):

workedSteps.text: The outer variable i takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, and for each value the inner loop makes i passes.
Row by row, the inner line therefore runs 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 times.
Adding the rows gives the total number of runs.
The formula n(n − 1)/2 with n = 6 agrees with the sum, which is the check to make whenever you have both.
Apply the same formula to n = 10 and enter the count.

steps.headline: Change the inner loop to range(i, n) and count the runs for n = 5: for i in range(5): for j in range(i, 5):

workedSteps.text: For i = 0 the inner loop runs j = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, which is 5 passes.
For i = 1 it runs j = 1, 2, 3, 4, which is 4 passes, and each later row is one shorter, so the rows are 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1.
This is the same staircase as before, read from the other end, so its sum is 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2. Use it for n = 100.

lead.text: Written out, n(n − 1)/2 is n²/2 − n/2. As n grows, the n²/2 part outgrows the n/2 part and decides the shape, while the factor ½ only scales it.

We say that a step count f(n) is **O(g(n))**, read as big-O of g(n), when beyond some value of n the count f(n) stays below a constant multiple of g(n). For n(n − 1)/2 the multiple is 1, since n(n − 1)/2 never exceeds n², so the count is O(n²), and the collection of counts that grow like n² is called a **growth class**.

afterFigure.text: Two points follow from the definition. A growth class describes how the step count grows and says nothing about seconds, because the seconds taken by one step depend on the machine, and that constant is exactly what the notation leaves out. And n(n − 1)/2 is not a *better* class than n² for being half the size: doubling n multiplies both counts by about four, which is the behaviour the class records.

lead.text: Suppose a program runs a double loop of n × n steps and then, separately, a single loop of n steps. The two blocks run one after the other, so their counts add: T(n) = n² + n.

As n grows the n² term pulls further ahead of the n term, so the lower term can be dropped, and T(n) is O(n²). The rule has three parts: add the counts of blocks that run in sequence, multiply the bounds of loops that sit one inside another, and keep only the term that grows fastest, without its constant factor.

reveal.text: At n = 100 the same program takes 10,100 steps, of which the single loop supplies only 100.
The step count is 3n, and dropping the constant 3 leaves O(n), so a second loop adds a factor only when its bound grows with the input.

lessons.title: Arrays and contiguous memory

blocks.text: Suppose an array of 8-byte elements begins at address 1000. The element `a[5]` is then at address 1040, and the computer finds it with one multiplication and one addition, 1000 + 5 × 8, without looking at any of the five elements before it, which is the reason arrays are the container most programs start with.

The layout that makes reading so cheap also sets the price of changing the array's shape. Every element must stay at its exact distance from the base, so removing or adding one in the middle forces its neighbours to move, and those moves can be counted.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute the address of any element from its index, and count how many elements move when you insert into or delete from an array.
intro.whyItMatters: Reading an array is cheap and changing its shape is not, and both facts come from the same layout.

recap.keyIdea: An array stores equal-sized elements in consecutive memory, so `a[i]` is at base + i × size and is read in constant time, while an insertion or deletion at index i moves every element after it.

blocks.text: You computed addresses from the base, the index and the element size, and saw that the calculation costs the same for every index. You then counted the moves in a deletion, n − 1 − i, and in an insertion, n − i, which makes the front of an array the expensive end and the back the cheap one.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks what happens when the array is full, and shows why appending is still cheap on average.

lessons.orientation: Compute an element's address from its index, and count how many elements move when inserting into or deleting from an array.
lessons.nextAction: Simulate a doubling dynamic array, total its copies, and explain why the average cost of append is constant.

lead.text: A computer's memory is a long row of numbered slots, each slot a byte with its own address. An **array** asks for one unbroken run of these slots and stores its elements in it one after another, every element the same size.
The address where the first element begins, here 1000, is the **base address**, and the position of an element counted from zero is its **index**.

afterFigure.text: Switch the figure to 4-byte elements and the neighbours are only 4 addresses apart, since each element now takes less room, so the gap between neighbours is always the size of one element.

diagram.caption: The gap between neighbouring addresses equals the size of one element. Use the buttons to change the element size.

reveal.text: Each element before index 12 pushes the start of the next one 8 addresses along, which the next screen states as a formula.

lead.text: Index i has i elements before it, each of the same size, so the element begins i × size addresses after the base: **address of a[i] = base + i × size**. For the array in the figure, `a[3]` is at 1000 + 3 × 8 = 1024 and `a[7]` is at 1000 + 7 × 8 = 1056. The calculation is one multiplication and one addition whatever i is, and the computer can then read the element at that address directly.

afterFigure.text: That is why reading or writing `a[i]` is a **constant-time** operation, written O(1): the [[step count|The number of times a chosen statement runs, as a function of n. Met in 'Counting steps in nested loops'.]] does not grow with i or with the length of the array. Reaching `a[900000]` takes the same two operations as reaching `a[3]`, with no walk past the elements in between. Python's list works the same way, except that a list stores a reference to each object rather than the object itself, so the arithmetic locates the reference, and the 8-byte references are what sit side by side.

reveal.text: The same two operations give an address for any index, which is why a lookup in a long array is no slower than one in a short array.

lead.text: An array has no gaps, because the address formula only works if element i is exactly i slots from the base. Deleting the element at index 2 from an array of seven therefore leaves a hole that must be closed, and it is closed by moving each later element one slot to the left, starting with the one at index 3.

afterFigure.text: In general the elements after index i are those at indices i + 1 up to n − 1, and there are **n − 1 − i** of them. The cost of a deletion therefore depends on where it happens, and for the first element it is O(n), a step count that grows with the length of the array.

diagram.caption: Everything after the deleted element moves one place left. Use the buttons to step through.

steps.headline: Remove the element at index 1 from [4, 8, 15, 16, 23] by shifting later elements left, and leave None in the last slot:

workedSteps.text: Copy the list so that the original stays unchanged, then start at index 1, the slot being closed.
The element at index 2 moves into slot 1, overwriting the 8 that is being deleted.
The element at index 3 moves into slot 2, and the one at index 4 moves into slot 3.
The last slot now holds a stale copy of 23, so it is set to None.
Count the assignments that moved an element. Enter the number.

reveal.text: The count is the whole length, which the next screen turns into a rule for any insertion index.

lead.text: Insertion is the deletion run in reverse. To place a value at index i in an array with a free slot at the end, every element from index i to the last one must move one slot right, starting with the last so that none is overwritten.

afterFigure.text: The count is **n − i** for n elements held, so inserting at the end moves none and takes constant time, provided there is a free slot, while inserting at the front costs n moves. Python's `list.insert(0, x)` pays exactly this cost, and its documentation lists it as O(n).

workedSteps.text: Start from the last element and move it one slot right, so that nothing is overwritten.
Move the elements at indices 4 and 3 in the same way, working backwards.
Slot 3 is now free for the new value, and 3 elements moved in all, which is 6 − 3.
Now insert at index 1 in the original array and enter how many existing elements move.

reveal.text: Both reads cost the same two operations, so the position of an item makes no difference to reading it, though it does to inserting or deleting around it.

lessons.title: Dynamic arrays and amortised cost

blocks.text: Appending 1000 items to a growing array, one at a time, makes the machine copy elements 1,023 times in all, which is only a little more than once per append, even though a single one of those appends copies 512 elements at once.
The copies can be counted exactly, both for an array that doubles whenever it is full and for one that grows by a fixed number of slots, and the two totals differ enormously.

diagram.alt: A row of eight filled slots with capacity 8, then the same eight elements copied into a new row of sixteen slots where the ninth element has been written and seven slots are free.
diagram.caption: One append copies 8 elements and buys seven appends that cost nothing extra. Use the buttons to see the array before and after.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to simulate a doubling array, total its copies, and explain why appending costs a constant amount on average.
intro.whyItMatters: Python lists, C++ vectors and Java ArrayLists all rely on this argument for their append.

recap.keyIdea: A dynamic array that doubles its capacity when full copies fewer than 2n elements across n appends, so appending has a constant amortised cost, while growing by a fixed number of slots makes the total quadratic.

blocks.text: You followed a doubling array through 9 appends and found copies of 1, 2, 4 and 8, then saw that the powers of two sum to less than twice the last, which bounds the total by 2n. Growing by 10 slots instead made the resizes evenly spaced and the total about n²/20, so the policy matters: only a growth by a fixed *fraction* keeps the average cost of an append constant.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson drops the idea of consecutive memory and links items together with pointers, which changes what insertion costs.

lessons.orientation: Simulate a doubling dynamic array, total its copies, and explain why the average cost of an append is constant.
lessons.nextAction: Build a chain of nodes joined by pointers, traverse it and reverse it, and say which operations it makes cheaper than an array.

lead.text: An array cannot simply grow in place, because the memory just after it may belong to something else. A **dynamic array** gets round this by keeping two numbers: its **size**, the number of items stored, and its **capacity**, the number of slots reserved. While the size is below the capacity, an append writes into the next free slot and nothing else happens.

When the size equals the capacity the array is full, and the append has to resize first. It allocates a new array with *twice* the capacity, copies every stored element across, and then writes the new item. This policy is called **doubling**, and the copy is the expensive part.

afterFigure.text: One append can therefore cost far more than the next. What matters is how often the expensive ones come, because after a resize the array has as many free slots as it has stored items, and all of those appends are cheap.

diagram.alt: An array with size 3 and capacity 4 that has a free slot, the same array full at size 4, and a new array of capacity 8 holding the 4 copied elements and the newly appended fifth one.
diagram.caption: Size counts the items stored and capacity counts the slots reserved. Use the buttons to follow an append through the stages.

reveal.text: The new total is 31, which is 16 more than for 9 appends and only 14 more than the number of appends, a hint of the pattern the next screen states.

lead.text: In the figure for 1000 appends the resizes copy 1, 2, 4 and so on up to 512 elements, each bar twice the one before. A sum of powers of two has a neat property: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15, which is one less than the next power, 16. In general, 1 + 2 + ... + 2^k is 2^(k+1) − 1, so the last copy is *larger than all the earlier ones together*, and the total is 1023 for 1000 appends.

afterFigure.text: The last resize happens at a size below n, so its copy is smaller than n, and the whole sum is smaller than 2n. Adding the n writes of the appends themselves, the total work is below 3n for n appends, which is under 3 writes per append whatever n is. The total cost of a sequence of operations divided by the number of operations is called the **amortised cost**, and here it is a constant. This is a guarantee about *any* sequence of appends, not about a typical or random one: no sequence can force more copying than the bound allows.

steps.headline: Simulate the growth of an array that starts at capacity 1 and doubles when full, through 6 appends:

workedSteps.text: Append 1: size 0, capacity 1, so there is room. Write the item, with no copy.
Append 2: size 1 equals capacity 1, so double the capacity and copy the 1 element.
Append 3: size 2 equals capacity 2, so double again and copy 2 elements. Append 4 then fits.
Append 5: size 4 equals capacity 4, so double to 8 and copy 4 elements. Append 6 then fits.
Add the copies made at appends 2, 3 and 5 and enter the total.

reveal.text: The exact total is on the next screen, so you can see how close your estimate was.

lead.text: Suppose the capacity starts at 1 and grows by 10 whenever the array is full. For 1000 appends that is 100 resizes copying 1, 11, 21, ..., 991 elements, an evenly spaced list whose average is 496 and whose total is 100 × 496 = 49,600 copies, about 50 times the 1,023 that doubling needed.

afterFigure.text: For a step of c slots there are about n/c resizes, and the average copy is about n/2, so the total is about n²/(2c). That grows as n² for any fixed c, so the average cost per append, about n/(2c), keeps rising with n, whereas doubling holds it constant. A **fixed amount** added each time loses to a **fixed fraction** added each time, because only the fraction makes the resizes rarer as the array grows.

diagram.alt: Two bars to scale for the total element copies. At n equal to 100, doubling copies 127 and growing by 10 copies 460. At n equal to 1000 the figures are 1,023 and 49,600. At n equal to 2000 they are 2,047 and 199,200.
diagram.caption: Doubling stays near twice n, while fixed growth climbs much faster. Use the buttons to change n.

steps.headline: Trace 25 appends when the capacity starts at 1 and grows by 10 slots whenever the array is full:

workedSteps.text: Append 2 finds the array full at size 1, copies 1 element, and the capacity becomes 11.
Append 12 finds the array full at size 11, copies 11 elements, and the capacity becomes 21.
Append 22 finds it full at size 21, copies 21 elements, and the capacity becomes 31, which covers append 25. Add the copies and enter the total.

lead.text: Real libraries use growth factors other than 2, and CPython's list uses one smaller than 2.

reveal.text: The pattern holds for any factor above 1, because the resizes still come further apart in proportion to the size, which keeps the total copying proportional to n.

lessons.title: Linked lists and pointers

blocks.text: In a linked list the node holding 7 sits at address 2040 and holds the address 1016, where the node holding 3 is stored. There is no formula that gives the address of the hundredth node from its position, so the only way to reach it is to start at the head and follow ninety-nine references.

That walk is what a linked list pays for a layout in which a node can be added after any node you hold by changing two references, with no element moved, and counting both sides of that trade shows which jobs suit a list and which suit an array.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to traverse, insert into and reverse a linked list by following its references, and say where it beats an array and where it loses.
intro.whyItMatters: Each container is cheap at some operations and dear at others, and choosing one starts from knowing which.

recap.keyIdea: A linked list is a chain of nodes joined by references, so reaching the k-th node costs k steps, while inserting after a node you hold takes two reference changes and moves nothing.

blocks.text: You followed references to reach a node and found that the cost grows with its position, which makes indexing O(k). You then rerouted two references to insert, learning that the order matters, and reversed a list in one pass, and you saw that the cheap insertion is only cheap once the right node is already in hand.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes two restricted ways of using a list, the stack and the queue, and what each restriction makes possible.

lessons.orientation: Traverse, insert into and reverse a singly linked list, and say which operations a linked list makes cheaper or dearer than an array.
lessons.nextAction: Use a stack and a queue to solve small problems, and say which end each one takes items from.

lead.text: The previous lessons kept items side by side in one block of memory. A **linked list** takes the opposite approach and lets each item live wherever there is room. Each item is stored in a **node**, which holds two things: the item's value and a **reference** to the next node, meaning the address where that node is stored. The list as a whole is known only by its **head**, a reference to the first node, and the last node's reference is set to `None` to show that nothing follows.

In the second view of the figure the four nodes sit in memory in a different order from the list. The order of the list is the order of the references and has nothing to do with the order of the addresses.

afterFigure.text: To reach the third node there is only one way, which is to start at the head and follow references.

reveal.text: The count is one fewer than the position, which the next screen turns into a rule and a cost.

lead.text: Visiting every node needs a variable that walks along the list. Set `cur` to the head, and while `cur is not None`, use the value in `cur` and then replace `cur` with `cur.next`.

afterFigure.text: Reaching the k-th node therefore takes k − 1 references, so the cost grows in step with the position. This is called **sequential access**, and it is the opposite of an array's [[constant time|The step count does not grow with n. Met in 'Arrays and contiguous memory'.]] indexing, so `list[i]` on a linked list is **O(i)** and not O(1). Searching for a value costs O(n) in either structure, because both must look at items one by one.

reveal.text: Reading near the end of a long list is slow, and the cost is the reason arrays are used when indexing matters.

lead.text: Suppose `p` refers to the node holding 3 in the list 7, 3, 9, and the value 5 is to go straight after it. A new node is created, and two references are changed. First, `new.next = p.next` makes the new node point at 9, which is where `p` pointed. Then `p.next = new` makes `p` point at the new node. The list now reads 7, 3, 5, 9, and no existing node moved.

afterFigure.text: The order of the two lines matters. Had `p.next = new` come first, the only reference to 9 would have been overwritten, and the second line would then copy `p.next`, which is now the new node itself, so the new node would point at itself and **the rest of the list would be lost**. The last view of the figure shows this. With the right order the work is two assignments whatever the length of the list, so inserting after a node you hold is O(1), unlike the n − i moves an array needs.

diagram.alt: Inserting 5 after the node holding 3 in the list 7, 3, 9. The first view shows the list, the second shows the new node pointing at 9, the third shows 3 pointing at the new node, giving 7, 3, 5, 9. The last view shows the wrong order of the two steps, which leaves the new node pointing at itself and cuts 9 off.

reveal.text: Reading the order as 'save the old reference, then redirect' is a good habit for any pointer change.

lead.text: A list can be reversed without creating new nodes, by turning each reference around. The loop keeps two references: `prev`, the node already reversed, starting as `None`, and `cur`, the node being handled, starting at the head. Each pass runs four lines: `nxt = cur.next`, which saves the rest of the list, then `cur.next = prev`, which turns the reference around, then `prev = cur` and `cur = nxt`, which move both references one node along. When `cur` becomes `None` the loop stops and `prev` is the new head.

afterFigure.text: The line `nxt = cur.next` has to come first, for the same reason as in insertion: once `cur.next` is overwritten, the only path to the rest of the list would be gone. Each pass costs a fixed number of steps and there is one pass per node, so reversal is O(n).

diagram.alt: The list 7, 3, 9, 4 reversed in five stages. Before the loop all arrows point forward. After each pass one more arrow is reversed, drawn in the accent colour, with labels prev and cur showing where the two references stand. After four passes the arrows all point backward and prev holds the new head.
diagram.caption: Each pass reverses one arrow, and prev and cur move one node along. Use the buttons to step through the loop.

steps.headline: Reverse the list 5, 1, 8 by hand, starting with prev = None and cur at the node holding 5:

workedSteps.text: Pass 1: save nxt as the node holding 1, point 5 at prev, which is None, then move prev to 5 and cur to 1.
Pass 2: save nxt as the node holding 8, point 1 at prev, which is 5, then move prev to 1 and cur to 8.
Pass 3: save nxt as None, point 8 at prev, which is 1, then move prev to 8 and cur to None, which ends the loop.
The new head is prev, so the list reads 8, 1, 5. Count how many next fields were overwritten and enter it.

steps.headline: Reverse 2, 6, 1, 8 and read off the third node of the result:

workedSteps.text: Pass 1 points 2 at None. Pass 2 points 6 at 2. Pass 3 points 1 at 6.
Pass 4 points 8 at 1, and cur becomes None, so the loop ends with prev at the node holding 8.
Follow the new references from the head, listing the values in order, and enter the value of the third node.

lead.text: The table collects the costs. Inserting at the front is O(n) in an array, which moves every element, and O(1) in a list, which only needs a new head, while inserting after a node you already hold is O(1) in a list and O(n) in an array.

afterFigure.text: The words *a node you already hold* carry the weight. A linked list does not make insertion in the middle cheap in general, because finding the place means walking there, which costs O(n), and only the final rerouting is constant.

diagram.alt: A table of costs for four operations. Array: reading by index is O(1), inserting at the front is O(n), inserting after a held position is O(n), and searching is O(n). Linked list: reading the k-th item is O(k), inserting at the front is O(1), inserting after a held node is O(1), and searching is O(n).
diagram.caption: Each structure is cheap where the other is dear, and searching costs the same in both. Use the buttons to compare.

lessons.title: Stacks and queues

blocks.text: After `s.append(3)` and `s.append(5)` on a Python list, the call `s.pop()` returns 5 and not 3, because it removes the item added last. Allowing only that end to be used turns an ordinary list into a **stack**, and allowing items to join at one end and leave at the other gives a **queue**.
Each rule settles which item comes out next, the newest for a stack and the oldest for a queue, so a problem can be matched to one of them by asking which item it needs next.

diagram.alt: Two views of the numbers 3, 5 and 8 added in that order. In the first they form a vertical stack with 8 on top, and only the top is used. In the second they form a row with 3 at the front and 8 at the back, and items are taken from the front.
diagram.caption: The same three items, held under two different rules. Use the buttons to switch between them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace a stack and a queue, check brackets and evaluate postfix with a stack, and choose between them from the order items must be served.
intro.whyItMatters: Undo, the call stack of a program and breadth-first search all rest on one of these two rules.

recap.keyIdea: A stack removes the most recently added item first and a queue removes the oldest first, and the rule about which end is used, and not the storage, is what makes each one useful.

blocks.text: You traced a stack and a queue on short sequences of operations, and used a stack to check that brackets close in the right order, a job that counting alone cannot do, and to evaluate a postfix expression. The queue's cost depends on its storage, since `pop(0)` on a Python list shifts every remaining element, whereas a deque removes from the front in constant time.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from order to lookup, and finds an item by its key in a constant number of steps with a hash table.

lessons.orientation: Use a stack and a queue to solve small problems, and state the discipline each one enforces.
lessons.nextAction: Place keys into buckets with a hash function, deal with collisions, and compute a load factor.

lead.text: A **stack** is a container with a rule about its ends: items are added at one end, called the top, and removed from the same end. Adding is called a **push** and removing is called a **pop**, and a third operation, **peek**, reads the top item without removing it.

This order is called **last in, first out**, written LIFO. A stack is a rule and not a kind of storage: it can be kept in a dynamic array, where push is an append and pop removes the last element, or in a linked list whose head is the top, and in both pushing and popping at that end are constant-time operations.

afterFigure.text: The rule is useful because many problems need the most recent unfinished thing first. An editor's undo undoes the latest change before earlier ones.

diagram.alt: A vertical stack. First 4 is pushed, then 9 is pushed on top of it, and then a pop removes 9 and returns it, leaving 4.
diagram.caption: Items go on and come off at the top only. Use the buttons to follow push 4, push 9 and a pop.

reveal.text: The pops return 5, 8 and 3, which you can check against the rule that a pop removes the top.

lead.text: A **queue** reverses the rule: items join at the back, in an operation called **enqueue**, and leave from the front, in an operation called **dequeue**. This order is **first in, first out**, written FIFO, and it is the rule of a line at a counter or of print jobs waiting for a printer.

afterFigure.text: A Python list is an array, so `lst.pop(0)` removes the front item by shifting all the remaining elements one slot left, which costs one move for each of them and so O(n). The class `collections.deque`, a **double-ended queue**, adds and removes at both ends in constant time, and it is what Python programs use for a queue: `append` at the back and `popleft` at the front.

reveal.text: Because removals follow the order of arrival, the dequeues return 4, 7 and 9 in turn if they continued.

lead.text: A string such as { [ ( ) ] } is balanced when every closing bracket matches the most recent opening one that is still open. That *most recent* is the stack's rule, so the check is a loop over the characters. Push each opening bracket. For each closing bracket, pop the top and check that it is the matching opener. When the string ends, the stack must be empty, otherwise some opener was never closed.

afterFigure.text: Counting alone cannot do this. The string ( [ ) ] has two openers and two closers of each kind, yet it is not balanced, because the ) arrives when the top of the stack is [, which is not its partner. The stack records the *order* as well as the number of the brackets, and order is what the check needs.

diagram.alt: The string { [ ( ) ] } read one character at a time. Opening brackets are pushed. After the three openers the stack holds {, [ and (. Each closer pops the top and finds its partner, and after the last character the stack is empty.
diagram.caption: Each opener is pushed and each closer pops its partner. Use the buttons to follow the string.

workedSteps.text: Read ( : an opener, so push it. The stack holds one bracket.
Read [ : an opener, so push it on top. The stack now has the square bracket above the round one.
Read ) : a closer, so pop the top and compare it with the partner of ). The partner is (.
Enter the bracket that was popped.
The two do not match, so the check stops at once, and the string is not balanced although each kind of bracket appears equally often.

steps.headline: Check ( ( ) with the stack method, and say whether anything remains at the end:

workedSteps.text: Read ( and push it, then read the second ( and push it.
Read ) : pop the top, which is a matching (, so no mismatch occurs.
The string has ended. Count the brackets still on the stack and enter the number.

lead.text: In **postfix** notation the operator comes after its two numbers, so 3 4 + means 3 + 4 and needs no brackets. A stack evaluates it in one pass. Push each number. At an operator, pop two numbers, apply the operator, and push the result.

afterFigure.text: When the operator is not commutative, meaning that swapping its two numbers changes the result, the order matters. The first number popped is the *right-hand* operand, so for 9 4 − the pop returns 4 first, and the result is 9 − 4 = 5, with 9 as the left-hand operand. At the end of a well-formed expression exactly one number remains on the stack, and it is the value.

diagram.alt: The postfix expression 3 4 + 2 * evaluated with a stack. 3 and 4 are pushed, the plus pops both and pushes 7, the 2 is pushed, and the times pops 7 and 2 and pushes 14.

reveal.text: The stack never held more than three numbers, which shows how little the method needs to remember.

lead.text: A stack, a queue and a deque are the same storage under different rules, and the choice is made by asking in what order the items must be served. If the most recent item must come out first, as with an undo history, the answer is a stack, and if the oldest must come out first, as with customers served in the order they arrived, the answer is a queue.

afterFigure.text: The calls of a recursive function wait on a stack, and a search that explores a graph level by level uses a queue, so recognising the rule in a problem is often the whole of the design.

diagram.alt: Three containers drawn as a row of three cells. A stack adds and removes at one end. A queue adds at one end and removes at the other. A deque adds and removes at both ends.
diagram.caption: The three differ only in which ends may be used. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The oldest waiting customer is always at the front, which is where a queue removes items.
A deque avoids the shifts, so removals at the front stay O(1) however long the queue grows.

lessons.title: Hash tables

blocks.text: In a table of 5 buckets the key 14 has remainder 4 on division by 5, so bucket 4 is the only place it can be, and a lookup opens that one bucket and nothing else. Python's dictionary works on this principle.
This works as long as keys do not crowd into one bucket, and with fewer buckets than possible keys some of them must.

diagram.alt: A table of five buckets numbered 0 to 4. A key is turned into a bucket number by taking the remainder when it is divided by 5. The key 14 gives bucket 4, and the key 21 gives bucket 1.
diagram.caption: The key is turned into a bucket number by arithmetic, so nothing is searched. Use the buttons to compare two keys.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place keys into buckets with a hash function, resolve collisions by chaining or probing, and compute a load factor.
intro.whyItMatters: A dictionary lookup that costs about one step is what turns many two-loop problems into one pass.

recap.keyIdea: A hash table computes a bucket from the key, handles keys that share a bucket by chaining or probing, and stays fast in expectation while its load factor, entries divided by buckets, is kept low.

blocks.text: You placed keys into buckets with the remainder rule, and found that collisions are normal and are resolved by keeping a chain in each bucket or by stepping to the next free slot. The load factor, entries divided by buckets, measures how crowded the table is, and a table resizes when it grows too high, so the expected cost of a lookup stays constant even though the worst case does not.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to functions that call themselves, and to the stack of waiting calls that makes them work.

lessons.orientation: Place keys into buckets with a hash function, resolve collisions by chaining or probing, and compute the load factor.
lessons.nextAction: Write a function that calls itself with a base case, trace the calls it leaves waiting, and count the calls of a function that calls itself twice.

lead.text: A hash table keeps its items in an array of **buckets**, numbered from 0, and a **hash function** turns any key into a whole number from which the bucket is chosen. For integer keys the simplest choice is the remainder after division by the number of buckets m, written k mod m. With m = 5 buckets, the key 12 has remainder 2, so it is stored in bucket 2.
Looking a key up repeats the same calculation, and the result says which bucket to open, so the lookup does not depend on how many items the table holds.

afterFigure.text: The array of the second lesson is doing the work here: a bucket number is an index, and indexing an array takes constant time. The hash function only converts a key, which may be a number, a word or a pair, into the index.

diagram.alt: A table of five buckets. Inserting 12 puts it in bucket 2 because 12 mod 5 is 2. Inserting 20 then puts it in bucket 0, and inserting 3 puts it in bucket 3.
diagram.caption: Each key goes to the bucket given by its remainder modulo 5. Use the buttons to insert the keys in turn.

reveal.text: Several keys sharing a bucket is normal, and the next screen names it and shows how a table copes.

lead.text: When two different keys give the same bucket they **collide**. A collision is not an error: the table has fewer buckets than there are possible keys, so some keys must share. The first way to cope is **chaining**, in which each bucket holds a list, called a chain, of every key that landed in it.

afterFigure.text: A lookup of 15 computes its bucket, 0, and then compares 15 with each key along that chain, first 20 and then 15 itself, until it finds it. The cost is therefore one calculation plus the length of one chain, never a walk through the whole table.

diagram.alt: A table of five buckets using chaining. After 12 and 7 are inserted, bucket 2 holds both. After all six keys, bucket 0 holds 20 and 15, bucket 2 holds 12, 7 and 27, and bucket 3 holds 3.
diagram.caption: A bucket holds a short list of the keys that landed in it. Use the buttons to see the first collision and the full table.

reveal.text: A lookup costs one calculation plus the chain length, so keeping chains short is what keeps the table fast.

lead.text: The second way to handle a collision keeps one key in each slot and moves a colliding key somewhere else in the array. With **linear probing**, a key whose slot is taken tries the next slot, then the next, until it finds a free one, and after the last slot it wraps round to slot 0. In a table of 7 slots with the hash k mod 7, the keys 31, 38, 45 and 52 all have remainder 3, so they cannot all sit in slot 3.

afterFigure.text: A lookup follows the same path as the insertion. It starts at the key's own slot and steps forward until it finds the key or reaches an empty slot, which proves the key is absent. The cost of a lookup is the length of that run of filled slots, so, as with chains, it depends on how crowded the table is.

diagram.alt: A table of seven slots using linear probing. The keys 31, 38, 45 and 52 all have remainder 3 when divided by 7. The first takes slot 3, and each later one probes forward to the next free slot, ending in slots 4, 5 and 6.
diagram.caption: A colliding key steps forward one slot at a time until it finds a free one. Use the buttons to insert the keys in turn.

steps.headline: Insert 10, 17, 3 and 24 in that order into a table of 7 slots, with hash k mod 7 and linear probing:

workedSteps.text: 10 mod 7 = 3, and slot 3 is free, so 10 goes into slot 3.
17 mod 7 = 3, and slot 3 is taken, so try slot 4, which is free.
3 mod 7 = 3, so slots 3 and 4 are taken, and slot 5 is free.
24 mod 7 = 3 as well. Probe forward from slot 3 past the filled slots, and enter the slot where 24 settles.

steps.headline: Insert 12, 19 and 5 in that order into a table of 7 slots, with hash k mod 7 and linear probing:

workedSteps.text: 12 mod 7 = 5, and slot 5 is free, so 12 goes into slot 5.
19 mod 7 = 5, and slot 5 is taken, so try slot 6, which is free.
5 mod 7 = 5. Slots 5 and 6 are taken, and the table has no slot 7, so the probe wraps round. Enter the slot where 5 is placed.

lead.text: How long the chains or runs get depends on how full the table is. The **load factor** is the number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets. Six keys in 5 buckets give a load factor of 6 ÷ 5 = 1.2, which means that an average bucket holds a little more than one key. Move the same six keys into 10 buckets and the load factor halves to 0.6, and in the figure the longest chain shortens from 3 keys to 2.

afterFigure.text: With a good hash function, which spreads keys evenly, the expected length of a chain is the load factor, so the expected cost of a lookup stays constant as long as the load factor is held below a fixed limit. A table therefore **resizes** when the ratio passes a threshold: it allocates more buckets, usually twice as many, and moves every key to its new bucket. The cost is the same one seen with the dynamic array, a rare expensive step that keeps the average cost of insertion constant. The guarantee is about the *expected* cost, and not the worst case, because if every key landed in one bucket a lookup would walk through all n of them, which is O(n).

diagram.alt: The same six keys, 12, 7, 20, 15, 3 and 27, in two tables. With 5 buckets the load factor is 1.2 and the longest chain has 3 keys. With 10 buckets the load factor is 0.6 and the longest chain has 2.
diagram.caption: More buckets for the same keys give a lower load factor and shorter chains. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: Python's dict is a hash table. Its lookups are expected to take constant time, which turns many problems that look like they need two nested loops into one pass. To find two numbers in a list that add up to a target, for example, you can keep a dictionary called seen of the numbers met so far, with their indices. For each new number x, ask whether target − x is already in seen. If it is, the pair is found, and otherwise x is stored and the loop moves on.

afterFigure.text: A key must not change while it is in the table, because a changed key would hash to a different bucket and could no longer be found, which is why a list, which can change, cannot be a key and a tuple can.

diagram.alt: The list 2, 7, 11, 15 with target 9. At the first element, 2, the needed partner 7 is not yet in the dictionary, so 2 is stored with its index. At the second element, 7, the needed partner 2 is found, giving the pair at indices 0 and 1.

lessons.title: Recursion and the call stack

blocks.text: The factorial 5! is defined as 5 × 4!, and the chain of definitions stops at 0! = 1. A Python function can follow the definition literally by calling itself, and the question is where all those unfinished calls are kept while the chain runs down to the end.
They are kept on a stack, one entry for each call, and the values come back up in the reverse order.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a recursive function with a base case, trace its call stack, and count the calls of a function that calls itself twice.
intro.whyItMatters: Recursion is how trees, divide-and-conquer sorting and dynamic programming are written in the rest of the course.

recap.keyIdea: A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller one until a base case returns, each call keeps its own frame on the call stack, and a function that calls itself twice can make exponentially many calls by repeating work.

blocks.text: You traced `fact(5)` and found six frames at the deepest point, each holding its own `n` while the calls below it wait, and wrote `flatten` by asking for the smaller copy of the problem. The call count of a doubly recursive function follows calls(n) = 1 + calls(n − 1) + calls(n − 2), which gives 15 calls for `fib(5)` and 41 for `fib(7)` because the same subproblems are computed again and again.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses recursion to sort a list by splitting it, sorting the halves and merging them.

lessons.orientation: Write a recursive function with a base case, trace its call stack, and count the calls of a doubly recursive function.
lessons.nextAction: Sort a list by insertion and by merging, count the comparisons, and see why merging gives n log n.

lead.text: Some definitions contain a smaller copy of themselves. The factorial of 5, written 5!, is 5 × 4!, and so on down to 0!, which is defined to be 1. In Python the definition becomes a function that calls itself: `def fact(n): if n == 0: return 1`, and otherwise `return n * fact(n - 1)`. A function that calls itself is called **recursive**, and each of its calls works on a smaller argument than the one before.

afterFigure.text: The line that returns 1 without calling again is the **base case**, and it is what makes the function stop. Without it, `fact(0)` would call `fact(-1)`, and so on, and Python ends such a runaway after about 1000 nested calls by raising a `RecursionError`.

reveal.text: Each waiting call holds its own copy of n, which the next screen draws as a stack of frames.

lead.text: When `fact(3)` calls `fact(2)`, the first call does not disappear. Python sets aside a block of memory for the new call, called a **frame**, which holds that call's own `n` and the place to resume. The frames are kept on the **call stack**, the same last-in, first-out structure as in the previous lesson, so the newest call is always on top. In the figure the four frames for `fact(3)`, `fact(2)`, `fact(1)` and `fact(0)` pile up, each with its own `n`, and the lower three are paused in the middle of the line `return n * fact(n - 1)`, waiting for the answer to the call inside it.

afterFigure.text: A call is not a jump that goes back to the start. When `fact(0)` returns 1, its frame is removed, and `fact(1)` resumes with that answer and computes 1 × 1, returns it, and is removed in turn. The frames come off in the reverse of the order they went on, and the last to finish is `fact(3)`, which returns 3 × 2 = 6. The depth of the stack, here 4 frames, is what limits recursion in practice, and it is why Python caps it at about 1000.

diagram.alt: Frames of the call fact(3) drawn as a stack. First four frames for fact(3), fact(2), fact(1) and fact(0) pile up, each holding its own n. Then fact(0) returns 1, and the frames below it return 1, 2 and 6 in turn.
diagram.caption: Each call keeps its own copy of n on the stack and waits for the call above it. Use the buttons to step from the pile-up to the unwinding.

lead.text: A problem suits recursion when it contains a smaller copy of itself. A list that may contain lists inside lists, such as `[1, [2, [3, 4]], 5]`, is one, because each inner list is a smaller nested list. To flatten it into `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`, go through the items of the list. An item that is a list is flattened by calling the same function on it, and any other item is added to the result as it stands.

afterFigure.text: In this function the base case is hidden in the structure, because a call on a list with no inner lists never calls again. In general there are three things to settle when writing a recursive function: the simplest input and what it returns, the smaller input of the same kind, and the way the answer for the smaller input is turned into the answer for the whole one.

steps.headline: Trace flatten([1, [2, [3, 4]], 5]), which loops over the items and calls flatten on any item that is a list:

workedSteps.text: The first call receives the outer list. Its first item, 1, is not a list, so it is added to the result.
The second item, `[2, [3, 4]]`, is a list, so the call `flatten([2, [3, 4]])` is made and the first call waits.
The second call adds 2, and then meets `[3, 4]`, which is a list, so it makes a third call, `flatten([3, 4])`, and waits. The third call adds 3 and 4 and returns `[3, 4]`.
The calls return in turn, and the first call adds its last item, 5, to give `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`. Count the calls made and enter the number.

steps.headline: Count the calls made by flatten([[1, 2], [3, [4]]]):

workedSteps.text: The first call is on the outer list, whose two items are both lists, so it makes two more calls.
The call on `[1, 2]` finds only numbers and makes no call. The call on `[3, [4]]` finds the list `[4]` and makes one more call.
Add up all the calls, including the first, and enter the total.

reveal.text: The tree on the next screen counts every call, so you can compare it with your total.

lead.text: A call with n below 2 is a base case and makes no more calls, but every other call makes two. The count therefore follows a recurrence: **calls(n) = 1 + calls(n − 1) + calls(n − 2)**, the 1 being the call itself. With calls(0) = 1 and calls(1) = 1 the values for n = 0 to 5 are 1, 1, 3, 5, 9 and 15, so `fib(4)` makes 9 calls and `fib(5)` makes 15.

afterFigure.text: Each value is roughly 1.6 times the one before, and a quantity that is multiplied by a fixed factor at each step grows **exponentially**: even `fib(40)` would make over 300 million calls. The cause is visible in the figure, where the warm subtrees are both `fib(3)`, and the function computes it twice without remembering the first answer. The recursion itself is not what is slow, since `fact` makes only n + 1 calls; the repeated work is.

diagram.alt: Call trees for fib. Each circle is a call labelled with its n, and a call with n of 2 or more has two children, for n minus 1 and n minus 2. The tree for fib(4) has 9 calls and the tree for fib(5) has 15. In fib(5) the subtree for fib(3) appears twice, which is repeated work.

reveal.text: Each count is the sum of the two before it plus one, which is why the numbers climb so quickly.
The calls only ever go down, so the stack grows until Python's limit stops it, and the stack, not the arithmetic, is what runs out.

lessons.title: Insertion sort and merge sort

blocks.text: Sorting the six numbers 5 2 4 6 1 3 by insertion slides each number left past the larger ones before it, and how much sliding there is depends on how disordered the list is. A list that is nearly sorted therefore costs very little.
A list in the worst order still costs about n² steps, though, and merging two sorted lists is cheap enough that a method which sorts the two halves of a list and merges them needs only about n log n.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace insertion sort and a merge, count the shifts and comparisons, and explain why merge sort takes O(n log n).
intro.whyItMatters: Sorting is the standard test of whether a method grows gently or badly with the size of its input.

recap.keyIdea: Insertion sort does one shift per inversion, so it is fast on nearly sorted lists and quadratic on reversed ones, while merge sort merges sorted halves over log₂ n levels of about n work each and takes O(n log n) at the cost of extra memory.

blocks.text: You counted shifts in insertion sort and tied them to inversions, which gave 9 for a mixed list, 0 for a sorted one and 15 for a reversed one. A merge of two sorted lists needs at most one comparison for each item but one, and merge sort applies it over log₂ n levels, so 16 items cost about 64 moves.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson sorts by partitioning around a pivot, a method that is usually faster still but has a bad case of its own.

lessons.orientation: Trace insertion sort and merge, count shifts and comparisons, and explain why merge sort takes O(n log n).
lessons.nextAction: Partition a list around a pivot, give quicksort's best and worst cases, and see the least number of comparisons any comparison sort needs.

lead.text: To sort a list by insertion, treat the first item as a sorted prefix of length one. Then take the next item, called the **key**, and compare it with the items of the prefix from the right. Each item larger than the key is moved one place right, an operation called a **shift**, and when an item no larger than the key is met, or the front of the list is reached, the key is written into the gap. The prefix is now one item longer. In Python the loop is `for i in range(1, len(a)):` `key = a[i]`; `j = i - 1`; and `while j >= 0 and a[j] > key:` `a[j + 1] = a[j]` and `j = j - 1`; and finally `a[j + 1] = key`.

afterFigure.text: Each time the key is checked against an item of the prefix, that is one comparison, and the check that stops the sliding counts as well, unless the front of the list was reached.

diagram.alt: Six cards, 5 2 4 6 1 3, sorted by insertion. A sorted prefix grows from the left. Key 2 slides left past 5, key 4 slides past 5, key 1 slides to the front, and key 3 slides past 6, 5 and 4, ending with 1 2 3 4 5 6.
diagram.caption: The sorted prefix grows by one card each pass. Use the buttons to follow the passes that move cards.

reveal.text: The count is 9, which is exactly the number of pairs in the list that are out of order, as the next screen shows.

lead.text: An **inversion** is a pair of positions i < j with `a[i] > a[j]`, that is, a pair that is in the wrong order. The list 5 2 4 6 1 3 has nine: the pairs 5 and 2, 5 and 4, 5 and 1, 5 and 3, 2 and 1, 4 and 1, 4 and 3, 6 and 1, and 6 and 3. A shift moves a larger item past a smaller one that was on its right, which removes exactly one inversion, and the sorted list has none, so the number of shifts equals the number of inversions: 9 here.

afterFigure.text: The cost therefore ranges widely with the input. A sorted list has no inversions, so it needs 0 shifts and only n − 1 comparisons, 5 for six items, which is close to n steps. A reversed list has every pair inverted, n(n − 1)/2 of them, which is 15 for six items and the same triangular count as in the first lesson, so it is quadratic. Insertion sort is not always slow: on data that is nearly in order it is among the fastest, and the figure compares the three cases.

diagram.alt: Three six-card inputs. For 5 2 4 6 1 3 there are 9 shifts, 12 comparisons and 9 inversions. For the sorted 1 2 3 4 5 6 there are 0 shifts, 5 comparisons and 0 inversions. For the reversed 6 5 4 3 2 1 there are 15 shifts, 15 comparisons and 15 inversions.
diagram.caption: The number of shifts always equals the number of inversions. Use the buttons to compare three inputs.

reveal.text: Each of these pairs would cost insertion sort one shift.
A merge never needs more than `len(a) + len(b)` − 1 comparisons, and it can need far fewer.

lead.text: Two lists that are already sorted can be combined into one sorted list without comparing every item with every other. The two front items are the smallest of their lists, so the smaller of the two is the smallest remaining item overall. Compare the fronts, move the smaller to the output, and repeat, and the output is sorted. This operation is called a **merge**.

afterFigure.text: When one list runs out, the rest of the other is already sorted and is copied over with no further comparison. Every comparison moves one item to the output, and the last item needs none, so merging lists of lengths p and q takes at most p + q − 1 comparisons. Merging needs a separate output list as long as the two inputs together.

diagram.alt: Merging the sorted lists 2 5 8 and 3 4 9 into one. At each step the two front items are compared and the smaller is moved to the output. The five comparisons produce 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8, and then the remaining 9 is copied.
diagram.caption: Only the two front items are ever compared. Use the buttons to follow the five comparisons.

steps.headline: Merge [2, 6, 7] and [1, 3, 9] and read off the fourth item:

workedSteps.text: Compare 2 with 1, and move 1. Then compare 2 with 3, and move 2.
Compare 6 with 3, and move 3. The fronts are now 6 and 9.
Compare 6 with 9 and move the smaller. Enter the fourth item of the output.

lead.text: Merging suggests a way to sort. A list of one item is already sorted, which is the base case. A longer list is split in half, each half is sorted by calling the same method, and the two sorted halves are merged. This pattern, which solves a problem by splitting it into smaller copies and combining their answers, is called **divide and conquer**, and the recursion of the last lesson is how it is written.

afterFigure.text: The number of levels is the number of times 8 can be halved before reaching 1, which is log₂ 8 = 3, and not 8. At every level of merging each item is moved once, so each level does about n work, and the total is about n × log₂ n.

diagram.alt: A merge sort tree for the eight numbers 5 2 4 7 1 3 2 6. Going down, each list is split in half until the lists have one item, which takes three splits. Going up, pairs of sorted lists are merged, and the top list is 1 2 2 3 4 5 6 7.
diagram.caption: The list is split down to single items and then merged back up, level by level. Use the buttons to see the two directions.

steps.headline: Sort [5, 2, 4, 7] by merge sort, and count the comparisons:

workedSteps.text: Split into `[5, 2]` and `[4, 7]`, and split each of those into single items. A single item is sorted, so the splitting stops.
Merge `[5]` with `[2]`: one comparison, and the smaller moves first. Merge `[4]` with `[7]`: one comparison.
Merge `[2, 5]` with `[4, 7]`: 2 beats 4, then 5 beats 4, then 5 beats 7, and the 7 is copied.
Add the comparisons from the three merges and enter the total.

lead.text: For n items, merge sort has log₂ n levels of merging, and every level moves all n items once, so the work is about n × log₂ n. Doubling n adds just one level, so the work grows a little faster than n, and the growth class is written **O(n log n)**.

afterFigure.text: Set that against the worst case of insertion sort, about n²/2. At n = 1024 merge sort needs about 10,240 moves and insertion sort needs 524,288, about 51 times as many. The price is memory, since each merge writes into an output list as long as its inputs, so merge sort needs extra space for about n items, which insertion sort, working inside the list itself, does not.

diagram.alt: Two bars to scale for n equal to 16 and to 1024. Merge sort moves about n times log base 2 of n items: 64 for n of 16 and 10,240 for n of 1024. The worst case of insertion sort is about n squared over 2: 128 and 524,288.
diagram.caption: The gap between the two widens quickly as n grows. Use the buttons to change n.

About 10 levels of merging and an output list of about 1000 items, which are the time and the space that merge sort costs.

lessons.title: Quicksort and the limit on sorting
lessons.reviewLabel: Quicksort and the limit on sorting

blocks.text: Partitioning the list 3 8 2 5 1 4 7 6 around its last item, 6, takes one pass and seven comparisons, and it leaves the list as 3 2 5 1 4 6 7 8. The 6 is now exactly where it will be in the sorted list, and it never needs to move again.

Sorting the two sides the same way gives quicksort, which is usually the fastest of the comparison sorts, the sorts that order a list only by comparing pairs of items, and which has a bad case of its own.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to partition a list by hand, say when quicksort is fast and when it is slow, and work out the fewest comparisons any comparison sort needs.
intro.whyItMatters: Knowing the worst case of a method is as useful as knowing its typical speed.

recap.keyIdea: Quicksort partitions around a pivot that lands at its final position and then sorts both sides, costing about n log n on balanced splits and about n²/2 on one-sided ones, and no comparison sort can beat about n log n because it must tell apart n! orderings.

blocks.text: You ran the Lomuto scan, which grows a region of items at most the pivot and swaps the pivot into place, so a partition of n items costs n − 1 comparisons. A sorted input with a last-item pivot gives the one-sided splits whose total is n(n − 1)/2, and the decision-tree count shows that sorting 5 items needs at least 7 comparisons however cleverly it is done.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson keeps keys in a tree so that a search discards half of the remaining keys at every step.

lessons.orientation: Carry out Lomuto partitioning, give the best and worst cases of quicksort, and compute the comparison lower bound for sorting.
lessons.nextAction: Insert keys into a binary search tree, read its traversals, and relate its height to the cost of a search.

lead.text: Merge sort does its work after the recursion, by merging. Quicksort does it before. It picks one item, the **pivot**, and rearranges the list in a single pass, called a **partition**, so that every item not greater than the pivot lies before it and every greater item lies after it.

afterFigure.text: The two sides are not yet sorted, but they are separate problems that are smaller, so quicksort sorts each by calling itself, with a list of one item or none as the base case. The pivot ends at its sorted position, which can be anywhere in the list and is the middle only by chance, and that detail decides how fast the method is.

diagram.alt: The list 3 8 2 5 1 4 7 6 before and after partitioning around its last item, 6. Afterwards the list reads 3 2 5 1 4 6 7 8, with 6 at index 5, the five items before it all at most 6 and the two items after it greater than 6.
diagram.caption: One pass places the pivot at its final position. Use the buttons to compare before and after.

reveal.text: The count is 4, which is the pivot's final index, and the next screen shows the scan that places it.

lead.text: The partition keeps an index i for the last item of the **at-most-pivot region**, which starts empty, at i = −1, and an index j that scans the list from the front up to the item before the pivot. When `a[j]` is at most the pivot, i moves up by one and `a[i]` and `a[j]` are swapped, which adds `a[j]` to the region. When `a[j]` is greater, nothing happens, and it stays in the region of greater items between i and j. In the figure, green cells are at most 6, and orange cells are greater.

afterFigure.text: After the scan, the region of items at most the pivot occupies indices 0 to i. The last step swaps the pivot with the item at index i + 1, the first of the greater items, and so the pivot goes to index i + 1, which is 5 here. The scan compares each of the other n − 1 items with the pivot once, so one partition of 8 items makes 7 comparisons and costs O(n).

diagram.alt: The partition scan on 3 8 2 5 1 4 7 6 with pivot 6. Green cells are at most the pivot, orange cells are greater, and blank cells are not yet scanned. After scanning two cells the green region holds 3. After four it holds 3, 2 and 5, and after all seven scanned cells it holds five items. The last step swaps the pivot into index 5.

j = 1: 7 is greater than 5, so nothing changes. j = 2: 1 is at most 5, so i becomes 1 and `a[1]` swaps with `a[2]`.
j = 3: 6 is greater, so nothing changes. j = 4: 3 is at most 5, so i becomes 2 and `a[2]` swaps with `a[4]`.
The scan is over. The pivot swaps with `a[i + 1]` = `a[3]`. Enter the value now at index 4.
j = 0: 6 is greater than 3. j = 1: 2 is at most 3, so i becomes 0 and `a[0]` swaps with `a[1]`.

lead.text: The cost of quicksort depends on where the pivot lands. If it lands near the middle, each side has about half the items, the recursion is about log₂ n levels deep, and every level partitions about n items in all, so the total is about n log₂ n, as for merge sort. This is the **best case**, and it is also the typical one for a list in random order.

afterFigure.text: The **worst case** comes from a pivot that splits the list into nothing and everything else. With the last item as pivot, a list that is already sorted does exactly that, because the pivot is the largest item and ends at the last index. A partition of 8 items makes 7 comparisons and leaves a list of 7, then 6 comparisons and a list of 6, and so on, for 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 28 comparisons, the triangular count n(n − 1)/2 of the first lesson. Quicksort is therefore O(n log n) on average and O(n²) in the worst case, and choosing the pivot at random makes the bad case very unlikely for any input.

diagram.alt: Two recursion shapes for quicksort. With pivots that split the list near the middle, each level handles about n items and there are about log base 2 of n levels. With a sorted input and the last item as pivot, each partition leaves one empty side and a list one item shorter, so the sizes go 8, 7, 6 and down to 1, giving 28 comparisons for 8 items.
diagram.caption: A balanced split halves the work at each level, while a one-sided split removes only one item. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: For a sorted list of n items the total is n(n − 1)/2, which is quadratic, however fast quicksort is on random data.

lead.text: A counting argument shows that no comparison sort can beat n log n. A comparison sort asks questions that can be answered yes or no, such as *is a smaller than b?*, and the figure draws every possible run of such questions as a **decision tree** for three items. The six leaves are the six orderings of a, b and c, and the longest path from the top asks 3 questions. A sort must reach the right leaf for every input, so its tree needs a leaf for each ordering.

afterFigure.text: A tree whose paths all have at most k questions has at most 2^k leaves, so sorting n items needs 2^k ≥ n!, that is k ≥ log₂(n!). For 3 items that is ⌈log₂ 6⌉ = 3, and for 8 items it is ⌈log₂ 40320⌉ = 16. The quantity log₂(n!) is close to n log₂ n, so merge sort and quicksort on average are about as good as a comparison sort can be. A sort can beat the bound only by not comparing: *counting sort* tallies how often each value occurs, but it needs small whole-number keys.

diagram.alt: A decision tree for sorting three items a, b and c. Each internal node asks a comparison, with a yes branch and a no branch, and each of the six leaves is one ordering. Every path from the top has at most three questions. The second view marks the path for an input in which b is smaller than c and c is smaller than a.
diagram.caption: Each comparison answers yes or no, and the six leaves are the six possible orderings. Use the buttons to see the tree and one path through it.

lessons.title: Binary search trees

blocks.text: A search for 7 in a binary search tree whose root holds 8 begins with one comparison. Since 7 is smaller than 8, every key on the right of the root can be ruled out without being looked at, and the search continues on the left.

Unlike a sorted array, such a tree can take in a new key without moving any other, and how much of binary search's speed it keeps depends on the shape the tree takes, which is set by the order in which the keys arrive.

diagram.alt: A binary search tree holding the keys 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 13 and 14 with 8 at the top. A search for 7 follows the path 8, 3, 6, 7, visiting 4 of the 9 nodes. A search for 13 follows the path 8, 10, 14, 13.
diagram.caption: Each comparison sends the search to the left or the right, so most of the tree is never visited. Use the buttons to see two searches.
