intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to insert keys into a binary search tree, read its traversals, and relate its height to the cost of a search.
intro.whyItMatters: Ordered containers such as database indexes and sorted maps are built on this idea.

recap.keyIdea: A binary search tree keeps smaller keys to the left and larger keys to the right, so a search follows one path and costs at most the height, which is about log₂ n when the tree is balanced and n when it is a chain.

blocks.text: You placed keys by comparing them down from the root, and read the tree in pre-order, in-order and post-order, finding that in-order always lists the keys in sorted order. The height, the number of nodes on the longest path, bounds the cost of every operation, and it depends on the order of insertion: 4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7 give height 3, while 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 give a chain of height 5.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses a tree stored in an array to get the smallest item out first, which is the job of a priority queue.

lessons.orientation: Insert keys into a binary search tree, read its three traversals, and relate its height to the cost of a search.
lessons.nextAction: Insert into and remove from an array-backed min-heap, and use a priority queue to take the smallest item first.

lead.text: Binary search finds a key in a sorted array by repeatedly discarding half, but an array is expensive to insert into, as the second lesson showed. A **binary search tree** keeps the same halving in a structure that can grow. Each node holds a key and has up to two children, a left one and a right one, and it obeys the **search-tree property**: every key in its left subtree is smaller than its own key, and every key in its right subtree is larger. In this lesson the keys are distinct.

afterFigure.text: The property tells you where a new key must go. To insert a key, start at the root and compare: go left if the new key is smaller and right if it is larger, and repeat at each node reached, until the place you would go to is empty, and put the new node there. The tree you get depends on the order of the keys.

diagram.alt: A binary search tree built by inserting 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4, 7 and 13 in that order. After the first three keys, 8 is the root with 3 on its left and 10 on its right. After six, 1 and 6 hang under 3 and 14 under 10. After all nine, 4 and 7 hang under 6 and 13 under 14.

reveal.text: The path through 4, 9, 7, 6 and 5 is the longest, and the next screen explains why this count matters for searching.

lead.text: Searching uses the same comparisons as inserting. To find 7, compare it with the root 8: it is smaller, so go left. The search visited the nodes 8, 3, 6 and 7, which is 4 of the 9 nodes, and the rest of the tree was never looked at. If the search reaches an empty place, as it does for 5, which ends beyond the 4, the key is not present.

afterFigure.text: The number of nodes on the longest path from the root to a leaf is called the **height** of the tree, here 4. A search, an insertion or a deletion follows a single path, so its cost is at most the height, written O(h). What matters, then, is how the height compares with the number of keys n.

diagram.caption: A search never goes deeper than the longest path. Use the buttons to see the height and a search that fails.

reveal.text: A tree of 7 keys has a search path of at most 3 nodes here, which is the saving that a balanced tree gives.

lead.text: To read every key out of a tree, the traversal has to decide what to do at a node and its two subtrees, and there are three useful orders. **In-order** visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. **Pre-order** visits the node first, then the left and the right subtrees, and **post-order** visits the node last. Each is a short recursive function that calls itself on the left child and on the right child, with an empty place as the base case.

afterFigure.text: In-order gives 1 3 4 6 7 8 10 13 14, which is sorted, because everything in a left subtree is smaller than the node and everything in the right subtree is larger. This holds for any tree built from the same keys, whatever order they were inserted in, so it is how a search tree prints its keys in order.

diagram.alt: The nine-key tree with each node numbered by the order in which it is visited. Pre-order gives 8 3 1 6 4 7 10 14 13. In-order gives 1 3 4 6 7 8 10 13 14, which is sorted. Post-order gives 1 4 7 6 3 13 14 10 8.
diagram.caption: The small number above each key is its place in the visiting order. Use the buttons to compare the three orders.

steps.headline: Read the tree from inserting 50, 20, 80, 10, 40, 70, 90 and 30 in pre-order, visiting a node, then its left subtree, then its right subtree:

workedSteps.text: Visit the root, 50. Then take its left subtree, whose top is 20.
Visit 20. Its left subtree is the single node 10, which is visited next, and then 20's right subtree, whose top is 40.
Visit 40. Its left child is 30, and it has no right child, so 30 follows and the left side of 50 is finished.
Next comes 50's right subtree, whose top is 80. Apply the same rule there, and enter the key that is 7th in the whole visiting order.

steps.headline: Read the tree from inserting 4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5 and 7 in post-order:

workedSteps.text: Start with 4's left subtree. Within it, visit 2's left child 1 and its right child 3, and then 2 itself.
Next comes 4's right subtree, in which 6 is visited last. Enter the key that is fourth in the whole visiting order.

reveal.text: The keys line up in a chain, which the next screen compares with a balanced tree.

lead.text: The same keys can give very different trees. Inserting 4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7 gives the balanced tree in the figure, of height 3, in which every search visits at most 3 of the 7 nodes. Inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 gives a chain whose height is 5, so a search for 5 visits every node and the tree behaves like a linked list. A tree is **balanced** when its two sides are roughly equal at every node, and then the height is about log₂ n, because a tree of height h can hold up to 2^h − 1 keys.

afterFigure.text: So a balanced tree with 127 keys has height 7, and with a million keys about 20, while a chain of a million keys has height a million. A search tree is therefore not always fast, and the guarantee of O(log n) has to be earned. The standard remedy is a **self-balancing** tree, such as an AVL tree or a red-black tree, which rearranges a few nodes by rotation after an insertion so that the height stays close to log₂ n. Sorted input is the dangerous case for a plain search tree, much as it was for quicksort with a last-item pivot.

diagram.alt: Two trees. The keys 4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5 and 7 inserted in that order form a balanced tree of height 3. The keys 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 inserted in that order form a chain going down to the right, of height 5.
diagram.caption: The same keys give different shapes depending on the order of insertion. Use the buttons to compare a balanced tree and a chain.

lessons.title: Heaps and priority queues

blocks.text: The array `[2, 5, 3, 9, 6]` is a min-heap: the smallest number is at index 0, and the number at each index i is no larger than the numbers at indices 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.
That arrangement lets a program take out the smallest item again and again while new items keep arriving, without keeping the whole array sorted and without scanning it each time.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to insert into and remove from an array-backed min-heap, and use a priority queue to take the smallest item first.
intro.whyItMatters: Schedulers, event simulations and shortest-path searches all rely on taking the smallest item next, cheaply.

recap.keyIdea: A min-heap keeps every node no larger than its children, stores a complete tree in an array with children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and supports insertion by sifting up and removal of the minimum by sifting down, each in O(log n).

blocks.text: You inserted by appending and swapping upward, so that 1 went from index 5 to the root of `[2, 5, 3, 9, 6]`, and removed the minimum by moving the last item to the root and sinking it with the smaller child. Both operations follow one path, whose length is the height, about log₂ n, and the heap guarantees nothing about the order of siblings.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from trees to graphs, in which items may be linked in any pattern, and finds the order in which a search reaches them.

lessons.orientation: Insert into and remove from an array-backed min-heap, and use a priority queue to take the smallest item first.
lessons.nextAction: Represent a graph as adjacency lists, and produce breadth-first and depth-first orders and shortest hop counts.

lead.text: A sorted array finds the smallest at once but is costly to insert into, and an unsorted one is cheap to insert into but costs a scan to find the smallest. A **min-heap** gives both operations a short path. It is a binary tree in which every node is no larger than its children, the **heap property**, so the smallest item is always at the root.

afterFigure.text: The tree is kept *complete*, with every level full except possibly the last, which fills from the left, and that makes it fit in an array with no pointers. Reading the tree level by level, left to right, gives the array, so the root is at index 0, the children of the item at index i are at **2i + 1** and **2i + 2**, and its parent is at **(i − 1) // 2**.

diagram.alt: The array 2, 5, 3, 9, 6 as a tree. The children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and the parent of index i is at (i − 1) // 2. The views mark index 1, whose parent is index 0 and whose children are indices 3 and 4, and index 4, whose parent is index 1.
diagram.caption: The index formulas replace the pointers of a tree. Use the buttons to see the relatives of two items.

reveal.text: The next screen shows the swaps, and the final array is `[1, 5, 2, 9, 6, 3]`.

lead.text: To insert an item into a min-heap, first put it in the next free slot at the end of the array, which keeps the tree complete. That may break the heap property, because the new item could be smaller than its parent. So compare it with its parent, at index (i − 1) // 2, and if it is smaller swap them, and repeat from the new position until the item is no smaller than its parent or has reached the root. This upward movement is called **sifting up**.

afterFigure.text: Each swap moves the item up one level, and it never needs to go further than the root, so the number of swaps is at most the height of the tree.

diagram.alt: Inserting 1 into the min-heap 2, 5, 3, 9, 6. The 1 is appended at index 5. Its parent at index 2 holds 3, so they swap. Its new parent at index 0 holds 2, so they swap again, and 1 is at the root. The final array is 1, 5, 2, 9, 6, 3.
diagram.caption: The new item swaps upward while it is smaller than its parent. Use the buttons to follow the swaps.

reveal.text: An insertion can stop at once, so the cost ranges from a single comparison up to one swap per level.

lead.text: The smallest item is at index 0, so reading it costs nothing, but removing it leaves a hole at the root. Filling the hole by shifting everything would cost O(n), and a different move keeps the tree complete. Take the last item of the array and put it at the root, which shortens the array by one. The tree is complete again, but the new root is probably too large, so it must **sift down**: compare it with its two children, and if either is smaller, swap it with the *smaller* of the two, and repeat from the new position until it is no larger than its children.

afterFigure.text: The swap must be with the smaller child, since swapping with the larger one would leave the smaller child below a larger parent, and the heap property would break.

diagram.alt: Removing the minimum from the min-heap 1, 5, 2, 9, 6, 3. The 1 is returned and the last item, 3, moves to the root. Its children are 5 and 2, and 2 is the smaller, so 3 swaps with it. The result is 2, 5, 3, 9, 6.
diagram.caption: The item moved to the root sinks by swapping with its smaller child. Use the buttons to follow the steps.

steps.headline: Remove the minimum from the min-heap [2, 5, 3, 9, 6]:

workedSteps.text: The minimum is the first element, 2, and it is returned. The last item, 6, is taken off the end and placed at the root.
The root 6 has the children 5 and 3. Swap it with the smaller child, provided that child is smaller than 6, and enter the first element of the heap after the swap.
The item 6 is now at index 2, and its children would be at indices 5 and 6, which do not exist, so the sift-down stops.

steps.headline: Remove the minimum from the min-heap [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5, 6]:

workedSteps.text: The minimum, 1, leaves. The last item, 6, goes to the root, giving `[6, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5]`.
The children of the root are 3 and 2, and the smaller, 2, swaps with 6.
The item 6 at index 2 has one child, at index 5, which holds a smaller value, so it swaps again. Enter the value now at index 2.

lead.text: A **priority queue** is a container with two operations: add an item, and remove the item with the highest priority, which for a min-heap means the smallest key. A heap does both by a path that follows the height of the tree. A complete tree with n items has about log₂ n levels, so a sift-up or a sift-down makes at most one swap per level, and both operations are **O(log n)**. A heap of a million items has only 20 levels, so no removal costs more than about 20 swaps.

afterFigure.text: A heap is not sorted, and it is not a search tree. Only the order between a parent and its children is guaranteed, so the second-smallest item is at index 1 or index 2, not always at index 1. Finding an arbitrary key means scanning the array, which is O(n).

diagram.alt: Three heap sizes and their number of levels. A heap of 7 items has 3 levels, a heap of 1,023 items has 10 levels, and a heap of 1,048,575 items has 20 levels. Each insertion or removal needs at most one swap for each level below the top.
diagram.caption: Doubling the number of items adds only one level. Use the buttons to compare three sizes.

reveal.text: The bound grows with the number of levels, so a million items cost only about 20 swaps.

lead.text: Python provides the heap as functions on an ordinary list: `heapq.heappush(h, x)` adds `x` and sifts it up, `heapq.heappop(h)` removes and returns the smallest item and sifts the replacement down, and `h[0]` reads the smallest without removing it. The call `heapq.nsmallest(3, items)` returns the three smallest items, and it is the sensible way to find the k smallest of a large collection.

afterFigure.text: The module builds a *min*-heap. To get the largest item first, a common trick is to push the negated values and negate them again on the way out.

reveal.text: A heap gives the minimum at once and the next minimum after one removal, and it promises nothing else about the order.

lessons.title: Graphs and traversal

blocks.text: Six towns, A to F, are joined by roads, and a program can keep the map as a list of neighbours for each town: A's list holds B and C, B's holds A, D and E, C's holds A and F, and so on. Nothing in the lists is a picture, yet everything the map says about which towns are connected is there.

Two questions come up about any network of this kind: which points can be reached from a given one at all, and which can be reached in the fewest steps. A program answers both by walking the lists from point to point, and the *order* in which it takes the next point decides which of the two questions the walk answers best.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a graph as adjacency lists, and produce the breadth-first and depth-first orders and the fewest-hop distances on a small graph.
intro.whyItMatters: Maps, networks and dependencies are all graphs, and these two searches are the starting point for most graph problems.

recap.keyIdea: A graph is stored as adjacency lists, breadth-first search uses a queue and so reaches every vertex by a path with the fewest edges, depth-first search follows one path as deep as it can, and both take O(V + E) when they remember the vertices already visited.

blocks.text: You stored a six-vertex graph as adjacency lists and found that its degrees add to twice the number of edges. Breadth-first search visited A B C D E F and gave A to F in 2 edges, while depth-first search visited A B D E F C and reached F by a path of 3 edges, so only the first guarantees a shortest path in edges.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson gives every edge a cost, and finds the cheapest path, which breadth-first search can no longer do.

lessons.orientation: Represent a graph as adjacency lists, and produce breadth-first and depth-first orders and the fewest-hop distances.
lessons.nextAction: Run Dijkstra's algorithm by hand on a small weighted graph, and explain why it needs non-negative weights.

lead.text: A **graph** has two parts: **vertices**, the things, and **edges**, the links between pairs of them. Towns joined by roads, web pages joined by links and tasks joined by dependencies are all graphs. In an **undirected** graph an edge works in both directions, as a road does, and in a **directed** graph an edge has a direction, as a link or a dependency does.

afterFigure.text: The usual way to store a graph is as **adjacency lists**, a mapping from each vertex to the list of its **neighbours**, the vertices it shares an edge with. In Python this is a dictionary, and an undirected edge appears twice, once in each endpoint's list. The number of neighbours of a vertex is its **degree**: B has degree 3, and D has degree 1.

reveal.text: The degree of B is 3 and the degree of E is 2, which will matter when the edges are counted later in the lesson.

lead.text: To visit every vertex reachable from A, keep a **queue** of vertices waiting their turn and a set of vertices already seen. Start with A in both. Then repeat: take the vertex at the front of the queue and visit it, and add each of its neighbours that has not been seen to the back of the queue, marking it seen. In the figure, visiting A adds B and C, visiting B adds D and E, and visiting C adds F, so the visiting order is **A B C D E F**. This is **breadth-first search**.

afterFigure.text: The queue makes the search work in layers, because the vertices added first are visited first. A comes first, then the vertices one edge from A, B and C, then those two edges away, D, E and F. The small numbers beside the vertices are these distances, and the first time the search reaches a vertex it has arrived by a path with the fewest edges. So breadth-first search finds the **fewest hops** from the start to every vertex: A to F takes 2, by A–C–F, even though F is the last vertex visited in the order.

diagram.alt: Breadth-first search from A on the six-vertex graph. A queue holds the vertices waiting to be visited. Visiting A adds B and C, visiting B adds D and E, visiting C adds F, and the rest add nothing. The visiting order is A B C D E F, and the small number beside a vertex is its distance in edges from A.
diagram.caption: Vertices are visited in order of their distance from A. Use the buttons to step through the search.

reveal.text: The visiting order is A B C D E F, so the last vertex is also the one that was added to the queue last.
The route D–B–E–F is the shortest, and the route through A is one edge longer.

steps.headline: Run breadth-first search from F, taking neighbours in their listed order:

workedSteps.text: The queue starts as [F]. Visit F: its neighbours C and E are unseen, so both join the queue.
Visit C: its neighbours are A and F, and A is unseen, so A joins the queue. Visit E: its neighbours are B and F, and B is unseen, so B joins.
workedSteps.math: visited: F, C, E     queue: A, B

workedSteps.text: Visit A: its neighbours B and C are both seen. Visit B: its neighbour D is unseen, so D joins the queue.
workedSteps.math: visited: F, C, E, A, B     queue: D

workedSteps.text: Visit D, the last vertex in the queue. Enter the vertex that is visited last.

lead.text: **Depth-first search** goes the other way. From the current vertex it takes the first unvisited neighbour and carries on from there, going deeper each time, and only when a vertex has no unvisited neighbour does it back up one step and try the next neighbour of the vertex before. It can be written as a recursive function or with an explicit stack in place of the queue. In the figure the search goes from A to B and then D, a dead end, backs up to B, goes on to E and F, and then reaches C, giving the order **A B D E F C**.

afterFigure.text: Depth-first search reaches every vertex that can be reached, but the path it follows to a vertex need not be the shortest. Here it reaches F by A–B–E–F, three edges, while A–C–F has only two. Depth-first search is the better tool for tasks that need to follow a path to its end, such as finding a way out of a maze or ordering tasks by their dependencies.

diagram.alt: Depth-first search from A on the six-vertex graph, taking neighbours in their listed order. It goes from A to B and D, and since D has no unvisited neighbour it backs up to B and goes to E and F, then on to C. The small number beside each vertex is its place in the visiting order: A B D E F C.
diagram.caption: The search goes as deep as it can before backing up. Use the buttons to follow the path.

reveal.text: Depth-first search reached F in three edges and visited it before C, though the shortest route to F passes through C.

steps.headline: Run depth-first search from P on P: [Q, R], Q: [P, S], R: [P], S: [Q]:

workedSteps.text: Visit P, then take its first neighbour, Q, and visit it. Q's first neighbour is P, which is visited, so go on to its second neighbour, S.
Visit S. Its only neighbour, Q, is visited, so back up to Q, which has no unvisited neighbour left, and then back up to P.
P's second neighbour, R, is unvisited. Visit it, and enter the position that R takes in the whole visiting order.

reveal.text: Each edge is written twice, so the entries total twice the number of edges.

lead.text: The degrees of the six vertices in the figure are 2, 3, 2, 1, 2 and 2, which add up to 12. Every undirected edge is counted at both of its ends, so the **sum of the degrees is 2E**, and with 12 entries the graph has 6 edges. This is also the amount of work a search does. A search handles each vertex once, when it is added to the queue or the stack, and goes through each adjacency list once, so it looks at every entry, which is 2E of them. The total is proportional to V + E, written **O(V + E)**, for both breadth-first and depth-first search.

afterFigure.text: That count holds only if a vertex is never handled twice, and this needs the set of visited vertices. The graph contains a cycle, A–B–E–F–C–A, and a search that does not remember where it has been goes round it for ever, as the figure shows. Checking the visited set costs a constant time for each neighbour, using a hash table, which keeps the total at O(V + E). The two searches differ only in the container that holds the waiting vertices, a queue for breadth-first and a stack for depth-first.

diagram.alt: A cycle of five vertices, A, B, E, F and C, searched without and with a set of visited vertices. Without the set the search goes round the cycle for ever. With the set each vertex is handled once.
diagram.caption: A graph with a cycle sends a search round and round unless it remembers where it has been. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: Counting stops treats every edge as one unit, so breadth-first search is enough, and the next lesson adds edges with different costs.

lessons.title: Cheapest paths with Dijkstra

blocks.text: In a graph whose edges carry costs, the routes S–A–C and S–B–C from S to C both use two edges, but they cost 4 + 1 = 5 and 1 + 5 = 6, so a search that counts edges, as breadth-first search does, cannot be relied on to find the cheapest.

Edsger Dijkstra's algorithm of 1959 adds up costs instead, always finalising the closest unfinished vertex, and it finds the cheapest route from the start to every other vertex provided that no cost is negative.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to run Dijkstra's algorithm by hand on a small weighted graph, and say why it needs non-negative costs.
intro.whyItMatters: Route planning, network routing and many scheduling problems are shortest-path problems on weighted graphs.

recap.keyIdea: Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly finalises the unfinished vertex with the smallest distance and relaxes its edges, which is correct when no edge cost is negative and takes O((V + E) log V) with a heap.

blocks.text: You ran the algorithm on a five-vertex graph, finalising S, B, A, C and D in turn, and found distances 0, 1, 3, 4 and 7, with the cheapest route to C using three edges where breadth-first search would stop at two. A single negative edge breaks the method because a finalised vertex is never revisited, and with a heap each push and pop costs O(log V), so the whole run takes O((V + E) log V).

recap.nextHook: The last lesson takes a recursive problem whose calls repeat themselves, and replaces the repetition with a table.

lessons.orientation: Run Dijkstra's algorithm by hand on a small weighted graph, and explain why it needs non-negative costs.
lessons.nextAction: Turn a recursive problem with repeated subproblems into a table, and show where a greedy choice fails.

lead.text: In a **weighted graph** each edge carries a cost, such as a distance, a price or a time, and the cost of a path is the sum of the costs of its edges. The cheapest path between two vertices is the one whose total cost is smallest, and finding it is the **shortest-path problem**.

afterFigure.text: The last lesson's breadth-first search counts edges, and treats every edge as the same, which is the right answer only when every edge costs the same. A method is needed that adds up costs, and not edges.

diagram.alt: A weighted graph with vertices S, A, B, C and D. The edges and their costs are S to A 4, S to B 1, B to A 2, A to C 1, B to C 5 and C to D 3. The second view highlights the route S, A, C, which uses two edges and costs 4 plus 1, which is 5.
diagram.caption: Each edge carries a cost, and the cost of a path is the sum of its edges. Use the buttons to see the graph and one route.

reveal.text: The next screen shows a method that finds the cheapest route without listing every route.

lead.text: **Dijkstra's algorithm** keeps a **distance so far** for every vertex, which begins at 0 for the start S and ∞ for the others, and a set of **finalised** vertices, whose distances are known to be best. Then it repeats two moves. First, finalise the unfinished vertex with the smallest distance so far. Second, **relax** each edge from it to a neighbour v: if the finalised distance plus the cost of the edge is smaller than v's distance so far, replace that distance.

afterFigure.text: In the figure, S is finalised at 0, which sets A to 4 and B to 1. The smallest unfinished distance is now B's 1, so B is finalised, and relaxing its edges improves A to 1 + 2 = 3 and gives C the distance 1 + 5 = 6. Next A is finalised at 3, and its edge to C improves C from 6 to 3 + 1 = 4. Then C is finalised at 4 and gives D the distance 4 + 3 = 7. The order of finalising is S, B, A, C, D, and the final distances are 0, 1, 3, 4 and 7, with D the farthest.

diagram.alt: Dijkstra's algorithm on the weighted graph, starting at S. Under each vertex is its distance so far. S is finalised at 0 and gives A 4 and B 1. B is finalised at 1, and A improves to 3 and C becomes 6. A is finalised at 3 and C improves to 4. C is finalised at 4 and gives D 7. The finalising order is S, B, A, C, D.
diagram.caption: At each step the unfinished vertex with the smallest distance is finalised, and its edges are relaxed. Use the buttons to follow the steps.

steps.headline: Run Dijkstra's algorithm from P on the graph with edge costs P–Q 2, P–R 5, Q–R 1, Q–S 7 and R–S 2:

workedSteps.text: Finalise P at distance 0, and relax its edges: Q gets 2 and R gets 5. S is still ∞.
The smallest unfinished distance is Q's 2, so finalise Q. Relax Q–R: 2 + 1 = 3 is less than 5, so R becomes 3. Relax Q–S: 2 + 7 = 9, so S becomes 9.
The smallest unfinished distance is now R's 3, so finalise R. Relax R–S: 3 + 2 is less than 9, so S improves. Enter the final distance of S.

steps.headline: Run Dijkstra's algorithm from W on the graph with edge costs W–X 3, W–Y 1, Y–X 1, X–Z 4 and Y–Z 9:

workedSteps.text: Finalise W at 0, and relax: X gets 3 and Y gets 1.
Finalise Y, which has the smaller distance. Relax Y–X, which gives 1 + 1 = 2 and improves X, and Y–Z, which gives Z the distance 10.
Finalise X at 2 and relax X–Z. Enter the final distance of Z.

reveal.text: Breadth-first search would stop at two edges, but the cheapest route has three, and that gap is why the weights need a new method.

lead.text: Finalising the vertex with the smallest distance so far is correct, for the following reason. Any other route to that vertex must leave the finalised set through some other unfinished vertex, whose distance so far is at least as large, and then it can only add costs on the way. If no cost can be negative, the other route cannot end up cheaper, so the smallest distance is already the best. The argument is **greedy**: it commits to the locally smallest choice, and the non-negative costs are what make the choice safe.

afterFigure.text: A negative edge breaks it. In the figure, the edges are directed, with S to A costing 3, S to B costing 4 and B to A costing −2. The algorithm finalises S, then A at 3, the smallest, and only afterwards finalises B and relaxes B to A, giving 4 − 2 = 2, but A is already final and is never revisited. The true cheapest cost to A is 2, by S, B, A, and the algorithm reports 3. Graphs with negative costs need a different algorithm.

diagram.alt: A directed graph with S to A costing 3, S to B costing 4 and B to A costing minus 2. Dijkstra's algorithm finalises A at distance 3 before it looks at B, so it misses the route S, B, A, whose cost is 4 plus minus 2, which is 2.
diagram.caption: A negative edge discovered late can beat a vertex that was already finalised. Use the buttons to compare the algorithm's answer with the true cheapest cost.

reveal.text: The algorithm's answer is wrong by 1, because it finalised A before it knew about the cheaper route.

lead.text: Choosing the unfinished vertex with the smallest distance is the job of a **priority queue**. Each time a distance improves, the vertex and its new distance are pushed onto a min-heap, and the next vertex to finalise is the one popped from the top. A pop and a push each cost O(log V). Every vertex is finalised once and every edge is relaxed at most once, so the total is **O((V + E) log V)**.

afterFigure.text: When every edge costs 1, the smallest distance so far is always the vertex at the front of a plain queue, and the algorithm turns into breadth-first search, with no heap needed. The heap is what lets the same idea handle costs that differ.

lessons.title: Dynamic programming

blocks.text: The call `fib(6)` makes 25 calls, and many of them repeat each other, and every repeat gives the same answer as the first time. The cost of the recursion in the lesson on recursion was mostly this repetition.

If each answer is kept when it is first found and read back afterwards, the 25 calls come down to 11. Putting the kept answers in a table that is filled in order does the same for problems where an obvious shortcut, such as making change by always taking the largest coin, can give the wrong result.

diagram.alt: Call trees for fib(6). The first has 25 calls, each a circle labelled with its n, and the same values of n appear again and again. The second is the tree when every answer is remembered the first time it is computed, and has 11 calls, with the repeated calls shown in green as quick look-ups that do not branch.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to turn a recursive problem with repeated subproblems into a table, fill it in order, and show where a greedy choice fails.
intro.whyItMatters: Dynamic programming turns many exponential searches into table fills of a size you can count.

recap.keyIdea: A problem with overlapping subproblems is solved by storing each answer once, in a memo or in a table filled in an order that makes the earlier answers exist, which turns exponential recursion into a linear or polynomial count, and a greedy choice can fail where the table cannot.

blocks.text: You counted that memoising `fib(6)` cuts 25 calls to 11, and wrote the recurrence best[a] = 1 + the smallest of best[a − c] for coin change, filling it from left to right. For the coins 1, 3 and 4 it gives 2 coins for 6 where the greedy rule uses 3, so a rule that works for the coins in a purse need not work for every coin system.

lessons.orientation: Turn a recursive problem with repeated subproblems into a table, fill it in order, and show where a greedy choice fails.
lessons.nextAction: Choose a container or an algorithm from the operations a problem needs, count its cost, and trace the standard algorithms by hand.

lead.text: The last lessons counted the calls of `fib`: `fib(6)` makes 25. Yet the questions it asks are only the seven values `fib(0)` to `fib(6)`. A problem whose recursion asks the same smaller questions again and again has **overlapping subproblems**, and the repeats are where the exponential number of calls comes from.

afterFigure.text: The remedy is to answer each question once. Keep a dictionary of answers already found, and at the start of each call look the argument up before doing any work. This is called **memoisation**, from *memo*, a note to oneself. The second tree in the figure is the result, with the repeated calls shown in green.

diagram.alt: Two bar charts of how many times fib(n) is called when computing fib(6). Without memory, fib(1) is called 8 times, fib(0) and fib(2) 5 times each, fib(3) 3 times, fib(4) twice, and fib(5) and fib(6) once, 25 calls in all. With memory, the counts are 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1 and 1 for n from 0 to 6, 11 calls in all.

reveal.text: Only nine different questions are ever asked, so nine stored answers would be enough to serve all 67 calls.

lead.text: With the dictionary in place, a call for an argument already stored returns at once. The first call to each value from 2 up to 6 does real work, which means two further calls, and the calls for 0 and 1 are base cases. Counting every call, the first plus two for each of the five computed values 2 to 6 gives 1 + 2 × 5 = 11 calls, in place of 25. The green circles are the calls that found their answer stored.

afterFigure.text: For `fib(n)` the count is 2n − 1 calls, one more than twice n, so the work is proportional to n, where it was exponential before. Nothing about the recursion has changed except the memory. The idea applies whenever the subproblems repeat, and it is the first of two forms of **dynamic programming**: memoisation works from the top, asking for what it needs, and the second form, the table, works from the bottom, filling in the smallest answers first.

reveal.text: Going from n of 6 to n of 7 adds 2 calls with memory and 16 calls without.

lead.text: A table suits problems with a natural order of sizes. Take coin change, where the task is to find the fewest coins that make a given amount from coins of value 1, 3 and 4. Let best[a] be that fewest for the amount a. The amount 0 needs no coins, so best[0] = 0. For a larger amount a, the last coin used is some coin c that is at most a, and the rest, a − c, was made in the fewest coins best[a − c], so best[a] = **1 + the smallest of best[a − c] over every coin c that is at most a**. This formula is the **recurrence**.

afterFigure.text: The recurrence refers only to smaller amounts, so fill the table from left to right, from 0 upward, which guarantees that every entry needed is already there. In the figure, best[1] = best[0] + 1 = 1, and best[2] = best[1] + 1 = 2, because only the coin 1 fits. At 3 the coin 3 leaves 0 to make, so best[3] = 1 + best[0] = 1, and at 4 the coin 4 gives best[4] = 1 as well. Filling an entry before the ones it depends on would use a blank, so the order matters.

diagram.alt: A table for coins 1, 3 and 4 with one cell for each amount from 0 to 6, filled from left to right. best[0] is 0 and best[1] is 1. best[2] is 2, from 1 + 1. best[3] is 1, from the coin 3, and best[4] is 1, from the coin 4. The cells for 5 and 6 are not yet filled.
diagram.caption: Each cell is built from cells already filled to its left. Use the buttons to fill the table as far as 4.

steps.headline: Fill best[6] for the coins 1, 3 and 4, given best[0..5] = 0, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2:

workedSteps.text: The coin 1 fits, and leaves an amount of 5. Its candidate is 1 plus the entry for 5.
The coin 3 fits, and leaves an amount of 3. Its candidate is 1 plus the entry for 3.
The coin 4 fits, and leaves an amount of 2. Its candidate is 1 plus the entry for 2.
Take the smallest of the three candidates and enter it as best[6].

steps.headline: Fill best[10] for the coins 1, 3 and 4, given best[0..9] = 0, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3:

workedSteps.text: The coin 1 leaves 9, and best[9] is 3, so its candidate is 3 + 1.
The coin 3 leaves 7, and best[7] is 2, so its candidate is 2 + 1.
The coin 4 leaves 6. Work out its candidate, take the smallest of the three, and enter best[10].

reveal.text: The table gave 2 coins for the same amount, so the greedy count of 3 is worse.

lead.text: The cashier's rule, always take the largest coin that fits, is called a **greedy** choice, and the last lesson used a greedy argument for Dijkstra's algorithm. Here it goes wrong. For 6 it takes 4, then 1 and 1, which is 3 coins, while the table gives 2 coins, 3 and 3. Taking the largest coin first leaves the amount 2, which the coins 3 and 4 cannot make.

afterFigure.text: The rule works for some coin systems, such as 1, 5, 10 and 25, and it fails for others, such as 1, 3 and 4. The table does not guess. At every amount it tries every coin that fits and keeps the best, which is why it is always right, at a cost of one table entry for each amount, times the number of coins. Another table of the same kind finds the longest common subsequence of two strings, the longest string of letters that appears in both in the same order, though not necessarily side by side.

diagram.alt: Two ways of making 6 from the coins 1, 3 and 4. Greedy takes the largest coin that fits each time, 4, then 1, then 1, and uses 3 coins. The table finds 3 and 3, which uses 2 coins.
diagram.caption: The coin that looks best at each step leads to a worse total. Use the buttons to compare the two methods.

Greedy would take 5 and 5 and be stuck with 1 left over, but the table finds a way by using the coin 2 three times.

questions.prompt: The line `count = count + 1` is inside an outer loop of 5 passes and an inner loop of 3 passes. How many times does it run?
hints: Each pass of the outer loop starts the inner loop again from the beginning.
Count how many times the inner loop runs in one outer pass, then ask how many outer passes there are.
The line runs once for every pass of the inner loop, in every pass of the outer loop.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The inner loop makes 3 passes for each of the 5 outer passes, so the line runs 5 × 3 = 15 times.

questions.onCorrect: The inner loop's 3 passes are repeated on each of the 5 outer passes, so the counts multiply: 5 × 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 5 by 5. The inner loop makes only 3 passes, so its bound is 3.
That adds the two bounds. The inner loop starts again on every outer pass, so the counts multiply.

questions.prompt: Use the formula n(n − 1)/2 for n = 10. How many times does the inner line run?
hints: Substitute 10 for n in n(n − 1)/2.
Work out 10 × 9 first.
Then halve the product.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 × 9 = 90, and half of 90 is 45.

questions.onCorrect: For n = 10 the rows contribute 0 + 1 + ... + 9, which the formula collapses to 10 × 9 ÷ 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is n(n − 1) before halving. The sum is half of it.
That is n² for a full grid. The inner bound here is i, so only the staircase of cells is counted.

questions.prompt: Use n(n + 1)/2 for n = 100. How many times does the inner line run?
hints: The first row has n runs and the last has 1, so the sum is 1 + 2 + ... + n.
Substitute 100 for n in n(n + 1)/2.
Work out 100 × 101 before halving.
questions.onCorrect: The rows run n, n − 1, ..., 1, which is the same staircase read from the other end.

misconceptions.feedback: That is n(n − 1)/2, the count for `range(i)`. Here the first row has n runs, so the sum reaches n.
That is n(n + 1) before halving. The sum is half of it.

questions.prompt: A program runs a double loop of n × n steps, and after it a separate single loop of n steps. How many steps does it take in total when n = 12?
hints: The two blocks run one after the other, so their counts are added.
The double loop contributes 12 × 12.
The single loop contributes 12.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The double loop runs 12 × 12 = 144 steps, the single loop runs 12, and 144 + 12 = 156.

questions.onCorrect: Sequential blocks add: 144 + 12. The double loop supplies almost all of the total, which is why only its term survives in the class.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the double loop. The separate single loop runs afterwards and adds its own 12 steps.
That adds 12 and 12. The double loop runs n × n steps, which is 144 here.

questions.prompt: `for i in range(n): for j in range(3): count = count + 1`. Write the growth class of the step count in big-O form.
hints: The inner loop always makes the same number of passes.
Work out the step count as a formula in n before naming its class.
questions.onCorrect: The count is 3n, which is a constant multiple of n, so the class is the same as for a single loop.

misconceptions.feedback: Nested loops give a square only when both bounds grow with the input. Here the inner bound is the constant 3, which only scales the count.
Nested loops give a square only when both bounds grow with the input. Here the inner bound is the constant 3, which only scales the count.

questions.prompt: `for i in range(9): for j in range(i): count = count + 1`. What is `count` at the end?
hints: The inner loop makes i passes on the pass numbered i.
The rows run 0, 1, 2, up to 8.
Add the rows, or use the pairing formula with n = 9.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sum 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 is 36, which agrees with 9 × 8 ÷ 2.

questions.onCorrect: The rows contribute 0 + 1 + ... + 8, which is 9 × 8 ÷ 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 1 through 9. The inner bound is i, which starts at 0 and stops at 8.
That is a full 9 by 9 grid. The inner bound here is i, so the count is smaller.

questions.prompt: A program takes 3n² + 5n + 20 steps. Write its growth class in big-O form.
hints: Find the term that grows fastest as n becomes large.
Drop its constant factor as well.
questions.onCorrect: The 5n and the 20 are small next to 3n² when n is large, and the factor 3 is a constant, so only n² remains.

misconceptions.feedback: The term 5n is smaller than 3n² for large n, so the class follows the n² term.
A constant factor does not change the class, so the 3 is dropped as well.

questions.prompt: A program runs a double loop of n × n steps and then, separately, a single loop of n steps. Which class describes its growth?
hints: The two blocks run one after the other.
Keep the term that grows fastest.
questions.onCorrect: Sequential blocks add, so T(n) = n² + n, and the n² term decides the class.

misconceptions.feedback: The single loop is O(n), but the double loop before it supplies n² steps and outgrows it.
Nothing in this program halves or doubles a range repeatedly, so there is no log factor. The count is n² + n.
A cube needs three loops nested inside one another. Two nested loops give n², and the added single loop does not multiply it.

choices.label: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(n³)

questions.prompt: An array of 8-byte elements has base address 1000. What is the address of the element at index 5?
hints: Each element takes 8 addresses.
Five elements lie before index 5, so count the addresses they occupy.
Add that to the base address.
questions.onCorrect: Five elements of 8 bytes lie before index 5, so its address is 5 × 8 = 40 past the base.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the index to the base, but each element before it takes 8 addresses, not 1.
That counts six elements. Index 5 has five elements before it, because indices start at 0.

questions.prompt: An array of 8-byte elements has base address 1000. What is the address of the element at index 12?
hints: Each element begins 8 addresses after the one before it.
The element at index 12 has twelve elements in front of it, each taking the same room.
Add the room taken by those elements to the base address.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Twelve elements of 8 bytes come before it, which is 96 addresses, so it begins at 1000 + 96 = 1096.

questions.onCorrect: Each of the elements in front of it takes the same number of addresses, so the position follows from the base, the index and the element size alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the index to the base address and ignores the size. Each element takes 8 addresses, so every step in the index moves the address on by 8.
That counts thirteen elements in front of the one at index 12. Counting starts at index 0, so twelve elements come before it.

questions.prompt: An array of 4-byte elements has base address 2000. What is the address of `a[9]`?
hints: Use address = base + i × size.
Here the size is 4 and i is 9.
Work out 9 × 4, then add the base.
questions.onCorrect: The formula needs only the base, the index and the element size, whatever the array holds.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the index to the base. Each element takes 4 addresses, so the index is multiplied by 4 first.
That uses 10 elements before `a[9]`. Only 9 elements lie before it.

questions.prompt: Removing the element at index 1 of a length-5 array, as above, how many elements move one slot left?
hints: The elements that move are the ones after index 1.
They run from index 2 up to the last index.
Count those indices.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The elements at indices 2, 3 and 4 move, which is 5 − 1 − 1 = 3 elements.

questions.onCorrect: The count is n − 1 − i = 5 − 1 − 1, one assignment for each element after the deleted one.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every element except the deleted one, but the element at index 0 is before the gap and stays put.
That stops short by one. Count every index from the first one after the gap up to the last.

questions.prompt: An array holds 6 elements and has room for more. A new value is inserted at index 0. How many existing elements move one slot right?
hints: The new value needs slot 0 to be free.
Every element currently in slot 0 or later has to make way.
Count the elements held.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All 6 elements, from index 0 to index 5, move right one slot to free slot 0.

questions.onCorrect: Inserting at the front means every element is displaced, so the cost grows with the length of the array.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the new value is written, but slot 0 is occupied, so every existing element has to move along first.
Nothing moves only when the value goes in the first free slot at the end, not at the front.

questions.prompt: The array `[4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]` has room for a seventh element. A value is inserted at index 1. How many existing elements move?
hints: The elements from index 1 onward must move right.
Their indices run from 1 up to the last index.
Use n − i with n = 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The elements at indices 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 move, which is 6 − 1 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: The count is n − i = 6 − 1, which is nearly the whole array because index 1 is close to the front.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for index 0. The element at index 0 stays put when the value goes in at index 1.
That is the number of new values. Every element from index 1 onward must move right.

questions.prompt: A Python list holds 1,000,000 items. How does the time to read `lst[900000]` compare with the time to read `lst[3]`?
hints: Think about what is needed to locate an element: the base, the index and the element size.
Does the computer pass over the elements before it?

acceptedIdeas: About the same, because the position is worked out by arithmetic
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About the same, because the position is worked out by arithmetic

questions.onCorrect: Indexing takes one multiplication and one addition, and it takes them for every index.

misconceptions.feedback: That describes a search, which walks past elements. Indexing computes the address directly and walks past none.
The distance from the start or the end has no effect on the calculation. It is the same two operations for every index.
That would be true if the list had to be walked from the front. The address is worked out in one step, whatever the index.

choices.label: About the same, because the position is worked out by arithmetic
Shorter, because the item is nearer the end
About 300,000 times longer, in proportion to the index
Much longer, because 900000 elements come first

questions.prompt: An array of 4-byte elements has base address 5000. What is the address of `a[12]`?
hints: Use address = base + i × size.
Work out 12 × 4.
Add the result to the base.
questions.onCorrect: The address is 5000 + 12 × 4, which depends only on the base, the index and the element size.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the index to the base, but each element takes 4 addresses.
That counts 13 elements before `a[12]`. Only 12 lie before it.

questions.prompt: An array of length 10 deletes the element at index 3 by moving later elements left. How many elements move?
hints: The elements that move are those after index 3.
Their indices run from 4 to 9.
Use n − 1 − i.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The elements at indices 4 to 9 move, which is 10 − 1 − 3 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: The count is n − 1 − i, which is 10 − 1 − 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the elements at indices 3 to 9. The element at index 3 is the one deleted, and it does not move.
That counts the elements before the gap. Only the later elements move.

questions.prompt:
`def remove_at(a, i):`
    `out = list(a)`
    `for k in range(i, len(a) - 1):`
        `out[k] = out[k + 1]`
    `out[-1] = None`
    `return out`

`remove_at([3, 6, 9, 12, 15], 2)` is called. What value is stored at index 3 of the list it returns?
hints: The loop runs for k = 2 and 3.
Find which assignment writes `out[3]`.
That assignment copies the element that was at index 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The loop runs for k = 2, 3. The pass k = 3 sets `out[3] = out[4]` = 15, and the last line then sets `out[4]` to `None`.

questions.onCorrect: The loop's last pass sets `out[3] = out[4]`, which copies 15 into slot 3 before the final slot is cleared.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the original value at index 3. The pass for k = 3 overwrites it with the value from index 4.
That is the value being removed, at index 2. The shifts write over it, and index 3 receives the element from index 4.

questions.prompt: A dynamic array starts with capacity 1 and doubles when full. Counting every element copy made during a resize, how many copies happen across 9 appends?
hints: A resize happens when an append finds size equal to capacity, and it copies size elements.
The capacities go 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on, so the array is full at those sizes.
Find which of the 9 appends meet a full array, and add the copies they make.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The array is full when it holds 1, 2, 4 and 8 items, so those resizes copy 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 elements.

questions.onCorrect: Appends 2, 3, 5 and 9 each find the array full, and they copy 1, 2, 4 and 8 elements.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the last resize, at the ninth append. The earlier resizes copied elements too.
That is the capacity after the last resize. The question asks how many elements were copied.

questions.prompt: A dynamic array starts with capacity 1 and doubles when full. Counting every element copy made during a resize, how many copies happen across 17 appends?
hints: List the sizes at which the array is full: 1, 2, 4 and so on.
The array is full at every power of two that is below 17.
Add the copies made at each of those resizes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The array is full at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16, so the copies total 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31.

questions.onCorrect: The resizes copy 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 elements, because the seventeenth append finds 16 slots full.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total for 9 appends. The seventeenth append meets a full array of 16 and copies 16 more.
That would need 33 appends. Seventeen appends reach only the resize at size 16.

questions.prompt: Using the table's rule, how many element copies happen in total across 6 appends?
hints: Find the appends that meet a full array.
They happen at sizes 1, 2 and 4.
Add the copies made at those sizes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 copies.

questions.onCorrect: Three resizes copy 1, 2 and 4 elements, and the capacity then reaches 8, which is room for the 6 items.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the copies at the last resize only. The earlier resizes copied 1 and 2 elements too.
That is the capacity after the resizes, not a count of copies.

questions.prompt: A dynamic array starts at capacity 1. Doubling its capacity whenever it is full needs 1,023 element copies across 1000 appends. If it grew by 10 slots whenever it is full instead, roughly how many copies would 1000 appends need?
hints: With growth by 10, the array resizes after every 10 appends or so.
Each resize copies about as many elements as the array holds at that moment.
questions.onCorrect: Growing by 10 gives about 100 resizes, each copying hundreds of elements, so the total runs to tens of thousands.

misconceptions.feedback: That holds for doubling, where resizes grow rarer. Growing by a fixed 10 resizes every 10 appends, and each copy gets longer.
That overshoots. There are about 100 resizes, each copying at most 1000 elements, and the average is about half of that.
That would be about 5 copies per append. Here there are about 100 resizes, each copying hundreds of elements.

choices.label: About 1,000, much the same as doubling
About 5,000
About 500,000
About 50,000

questions.prompt: An array starts at capacity 1 and grows by 10 slots when full. How many element copies happen in total across 25 appends?
hints: Find the sizes at which the array is full: it starts at 1, then 11, then 21.
The array holds 21 items when it next fills, and the capacity stays at 31 for the remaining appends.
Add the copies at those resizes.
questions.onCorrect: The resizes copy 1, 11 and 21 elements, and the capacity of 31 then covers all 25 items.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the resizes. The question asks for the elements copied by them.
That adds a copy of 31, but the capacity of 31 is not reached by 25 appends, so no resize happens there.

questions.prompt: A different array starts at capacity 1 and *triples* its capacity when full. How many element copies happen in total across 9 appends?
hints: The capacities go 1, 3, 9, and the array is full when its size equals the capacity.
Check whether the ninth append meets a full array, or whether the capacity of 9 already holds it.
Add the copies at the resizes that do occur.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Append 2 copies 1 element and makes capacity 3, append 4 copies 3 and makes capacity 9, and capacity 9 holds all 9 items, so the total is 1 + 3 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: Any growth factor above 1 keeps the copy total proportional to n, so tripling shows the same pattern as doubling.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds a copy of 9, but the capacity of 9 holds the ninth item, so no further resize happens.
That is the total for doubling. Tripling resizes at different sizes.

questions.prompt: An array starts at capacity 1 and doubles when full. How many element copies happen in total across 33 appends?
hints: The array is full at sizes 1, 2, 4 and so on, and each resize copies that many.
The thirty-third append is the first to find a full array of 32.
Add the copies at every resize from size 1 up to size 32.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The resizes copy 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 = 63 elements.

questions.onCorrect: The thirty-third append meets a full array of 32 and copies 32 more elements.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total for 17 appends. The thirty-third append meets a full array of 32.
That is the last resize only. The earlier ones copied elements as well.

questions.prompt: An array starts at capacity 1 and grows by 10 slots when full. How many element copies happen in total across 500 appends?
hints: The resizes happen at sizes 1, 11, 21, and so on, in steps of 10.
The last resize before the 500th append happens at size 491.
Count the sizes, then multiply that count by their average.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 50 resizes, averaging (1 + 491) ÷ 2 = 246 copies, and 50 × 246 = 12300.

questions.onCorrect: The sizes are 1, 11, ..., 491, which is 50 evenly spaced values with average 246.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the doubling total for 1000 appends. Growing by 10 resizes far more often.
That counts the appends. The question asks for element copies made during resizes.

questions.prompt: The total cost of a sequence of operations divided by the number of operations is called the ____ cost.
hints: The word describes a cost spread over the whole sequence.
It starts with the letter a.
questions.onCorrect: A single operation can be expensive while the amortised cost per operation stays small, and the guarantee holds for any sequence of operations.

misconceptions.feedback: Plain averaging over random inputs is a different idea. This term is a guarantee over any sequence, and it has its own name.

questions.prompt: A linked list has a head reference and 6 nodes. How many next references must be followed from the head to reach the 5th node?
hints: The head already refers to the 1st node, so no reference is followed to reach it.
Each reference followed moves from one node to the one after.
Count the moves from the 1st node to the 5th.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Moving from the 1st node to the 5th takes 5 − 1 = 4 references.

questions.onCorrect: The head gives the 1st node for free, and each further node costs one reference, so the 5th node needs one fewer than five.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the head as a reference followed, but the head already refers to the 1st node.
That is the length of the list. The question asks only for the moves needed to reach the 5th node.

questions.prompt: A linked list has 12 nodes. How many references must be followed from the head to reach the last node?
hints: The head refers to the 1st node, which costs no reference.
Each reference followed reaches the next node.
The last node is the 12th.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 12th node is reached after 12 − 1 = 11 references.

questions.onCorrect: One reference is followed for each node after the first, which is why access cost grows with the position.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the head as a step. The head already refers to the 1st node.
One reference reaches only the 2nd node. The last node is much further along the chain.

questions.prompt: Which pair of lines, run in this order, inserts the node new after the node p without losing the rest of the list?
hints: The new node must keep a way to reach the old next node.
Save p's current reference in the new node before p's reference is overwritten.
questions.onCorrect: Copying `p.next` into the new node first keeps the tail reachable, and only then is `p` redirected.

misconceptions.feedback: The first line overwrites `p.next`, so the second line copies the new node's own address, and the tail is lost.
Without a reference from the new node to the old next node, the rest of the list is cut off.
That makes the new node point back at p instead of forward at the old next node, which forms a loop.

choices.label: `p.next = new`, then `new.next = p.next`
`new.next = p.next`, then `p.next = new`
`p.next = new`, and nothing else
`new.next = p`, then `p.next = new`

questions.prompt: A list of 3 nodes is reversed with the loop of four lines per pass. How many times is a node's next field overwritten in the whole reversal?
hints: The line `cur.next = prev` runs once per pass.
Each pass handles one node.
Count the passes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There is one pass per node, and each pass overwrites one next field, so 3 passes make 3 overwrites.

questions.onCorrect: The line `cur.next = prev` runs once for each node, so the work of reversal grows in step with the length of the list.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the four lines of the loop body. Only one of them, `cur.next = prev`, overwrites a `next` field.
That multiplies lines by passes. Only the line `cur.next = prev` overwrites a `next` field.

questions.prompt: The list 2, 6, 1, 8 is reversed in place. What is the value of the third node of the reversed list?
hints: The reversed list reads from the original last node back to the first.
Write the original list from the end: 8, 1, ...
Count to the third value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The reversed list is 8, 1, 6, 2, and its third node holds 6.

questions.onCorrect: Reversal turns the order end to end, so the third node of the reversed list is the second node of the original.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the second node of the reversed list. Count from the new head, 8, and take the third value.

questions.prompt: A linked list holds n values in sorted order. A new value must be inserted in its sorted position, starting from the head. Write the cost of the whole operation in big-O form.
hints: The rerouting itself costs a fixed number of steps.
What must happen before the rerouting can start?
Finding the place means following references from the head.
questions.onCorrect: Finding the position costs O(n), and the O(1) insertion adds nothing to the class.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the cost once the right node is in hand. The walk that finds it comes first.

questions.prompt: A linked list has a head reference and 20 nodes. How many next references must be followed from the head to reach the 9th node?
hints: The head refers to the 1st node without following any reference.
Each further node costs one reference.
The length of the list does not matter, only the position.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Reaching the 9th node takes 9 − 1 = 8 references.

questions.onCorrect: The cost depends only on the position, not on the length of the list.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the head as a reference followed.

questions.prompt: The list 6, 2, 9, 5, 1 is reversed in place. What is the value of the second node of the reversed list?
hints: Write the original values in reverse order.
The new head is the original last node.
Take the second value of that new order.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The reversed list is 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, and its second node holds 5.

questions.onCorrect: Reversal turns the list end to end, so the reversed list reads 1, 5, 9, 2, 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first node of the reversed list, the new head.
That is the second node of the original list, not of the reversed one.

questions.prompt: What is the cost, in big-O form, of inserting a new value at the front of a linked list of n nodes?
hints: Only the new node and the head change.
The existing nodes do not move.
questions.onCorrect: The new node points at the old head, and the head refers to the new node, which is two assignments whatever n is.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the cost for an array, where every element shifts. A list needs only the new node and the head to change.

questions.prompt: Start with an empty stack and do: push 3, push 5, pop, push 8, pop, pop. What value does the last pop return?
hints: Track the stack after each operation, and remember that a pop removes the most recently added item that is still there.
Write the contents of the stack from bottom to top after each step.
questions.onCorrect: The pops return 5, then 8, then 3, in the reverse of the order the items were pushed, apart from the interleaving.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value returned by the second pop. The question asks about the last pop, which is the third.
That is the value returned by the first pop. The question asks about the last pop.

questions.prompt: A queue is empty. The operations are: enqueue 4, enqueue 7, enqueue 9, dequeue, dequeue. What does the second dequeue return?
hints: A dequeue removes from the front, where the oldest item waits.
After the first dequeue, the oldest remaining item is the next to leave.
Write the queue from front to back after each operation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first dequeue returns 4, and the second returns the next-oldest item, which is 7.

questions.onCorrect: A dequeue always takes the oldest item still waiting, so the removals come out in the order of the enqueues.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the answer a stack would give. A queue removes from the front, and the oldest item is nearer the front than the newest.
That is what the first dequeue returns. The second dequeue returns the next oldest item.

questions.prompt: Check the string ( [ ) ] with the stack method. When the first ) is read, which bracket is popped from the top?
hints: Push the first two characters and look at the stack.
The top of the stack is the one pushed last.
questions.onCorrect: The popped bracket is a square one, so it does not match the round closer and the string is rejected at once.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the bracket that was pushed first. A pop takes the top, which is the one pushed last.

questions.prompt: Check the string ( ( ) with the stack method. When the whole string has been read, how many brackets are left on the stack?
hints: Each opener is pushed, and each closer pops one opener.
There are two openers and one closer.
Subtract the pops from the pushes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two pushes and one pop leave 2 − 1 = 1 bracket on the stack.

questions.onCorrect: A leftover opener means the string ends with a bracket still open, so it is not balanced even though no mismatch was found.

misconceptions.feedback: That would need a second closer. Two openers were pushed and only one was popped.
That counts the pushes alone. The one closer pops an opener.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the postfix expression 6 1 2 + 4 * + 3 − with a stack. What is its value?
hints: Push 6, 1 and 2, then apply the first operator to the two numbers on top.
The + gives 3, and the * then multiplies that by 4. Continue with the next operator.
The last operator is a minus, and the first number popped is the right-hand operand.
questions.onCorrect: Each operator works on the two numbers on top, and the final minus has 18 on its left and 3 on its right.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value before the final subtraction. The last operator, minus, still has to take 3 away.
That stops after the multiplication. The later + and − still have to be applied.

questions.prompt: Customers at a help desk are to be served strictly in the order they arrived. Which structure fits?
hints: Ask which customer must be served first: the newest or the oldest.
Which rule takes the oldest item out first?
questions.onCorrect: Serving by arrival order is the FIFO rule, and a deque gives constant-time operations at both ends.

misconceptions.feedback: A stack would serve the newest arrival first, which is the opposite of the order wanted.
Sorting would put the customers in value order, and arrival order is not a value stored in the data.
A hash table finds items by key and keeps no order of arrival.

Sorted array
Stack
Queue

questions.prompt: A queue is kept in a Python list, and each dequeue is `lst.pop(0)`. The queue holds 1000 items in one case and 10 in another. How does the work for one dequeue compare?
hints: A Python list keeps its items in consecutive slots, so removing the item at the front leaves a gap there.
Think about what has to happen to each item behind the one that was removed.
Compare the number of items behind the removed one in the two queues.

acceptedIdeas: About 100 times as much with 1000 items, because every remaining item shifts one slot left
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 100 times as much with 1000 items, because every remaining item shifts one slot left

questions.onCorrect: A removal at the front of an array costs one move for each remaining element, which is why a deque is used for queues.

misconceptions.feedback: The call is a single pop, but the list is an array with no gap allowed at the front, so every item behind the removed one shifts one slot left. A deque avoids those shifts and a list does not.
The gap at the front is closed by moving every item behind it, not only the first few, because the items must stay in consecutive slots.

choices.label: About 100 times as much with 1000 items, because every remaining item shifts one slot left
The same, because removing one item is a single operation
A little more with 1000 items, because only the first few items have to move

questions.prompt: A stack is used to check { [ ( ) ] }. What is the largest number of brackets on the stack at any moment?
hints: Count the brackets on the stack after each character.
The three openers come before any closer.
The stack shrinks once the closers start.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: After the three openers the stack holds 3 brackets, and then each closer removes one, so the maximum is 3.

questions.onCorrect: The depth rises to the number of openers read before the first closer, and then falls with each match.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the length of the string. Closers remove brackets, so the stack never holds all six.
The stack holds a third bracket after the third opener, before any closer arrives.

questions.prompt: Start with an empty stack and do: push 6, push 2, pop, push 4, pop, pop. What value does the last pop return?
hints: Write the stack after each operation.
Each pop removes the item added most recently that is still on the stack.
questions.onCorrect: The pops return 2, 4 and 6, and 6 is the item pushed first, so it comes out last.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first pop. The question asks about the third.
That is the second pop. The last pop returns the item at the bottom.

questions.prompt: Which structure suits an undo history in an editor?
hints: Undo reverses the most recent change first.
Which rule returns the newest item first?
questions.onCorrect: Undo takes back the latest change before earlier ones, which is last in, first out.

misconceptions.feedback: A queue would undo the oldest change first, which would break the document.
A hash table finds items by key and keeps no order of recency.
A sorted array orders items by value, not by when they were made.

choices.label: Sorted array
Hash table
Stack
Queue

questions.prompt: A table has 5 buckets, and the hash is k mod 5. The keys 12, 7, 20, 15, 3 and 27 are inserted. How many of them go to bucket 2?
hints: Work out each key's remainder when divided by 5.
The remainder of 12 is 2. Check the other five keys the same way.
Count the keys whose remainder is 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12, 7 and 27 each leave remainder 2 when divided by 5, and the other three keys do not, so 3 keys go to bucket 2.

questions.onCorrect: Three keys share bucket 2, which already shows that a table with fewer buckets than keys cannot keep every key apart.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only 12. Check 7 and 27, which also leave a remainder of 2 on division by 5.
Two of them share the bucket, but a third key shares it as well. Check every key's remainder.

questions.prompt: A hash table with 5 buckets and the hash k mod 5 stores 12, 7, 20, 15, 3 and 27 with chaining, and bucket 2 holds the chain 12, 7, 27 in that order. To look up 27, how many keys are compared with 27, counting the match itself?
hints: Only bucket 2 is examined, and its keys are compared in order.
27 is the last key in the chain.
Count the keys from the start of the chain to 27.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The chain is 12, 7, 27, and 27 is the third, so 3 keys are compared.

questions.onCorrect: The comparisons run along the chain until the key is found, so a longer chain means a longer lookup.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be so if 27 were first in its chain. It is last, so 12 and 7 are compared first.

questions.prompt: Linear probing in a table of 7 slots with hash k mod 7. The keys 10, 17 and 3 are already in slots 3, 4 and 5. In which slot does 24 end up?
hints: Work out 24 mod 7 to find the first slot to try.
If that slot is taken, try the next one.
Slots 3, 4 and 5 are taken, so find the first free slot after them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 24 mod 7 = 3, and slots 3, 4 and 5 are taken, so 24 settles in slot 6.

questions.onCorrect: Each key stops at the first free slot from its own, so four keys with the same remainder fill four slots in a row.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the slot 24 tries first, but it is already taken by 10.

questions.prompt: Linear probing in a table of 7 slots with hash k mod 7. Insert 12, 19 and 5 in that order. In which slot does 5 end up?
hints: Work out the remainder of each key on division by 7.
12 takes slot 5, and 19 then probes from slot 5 to the next free slot.
After the last slot the probe wraps round to the first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All three keys have remainder 5. The first takes slot 5, the second slot 6, and the third finds both taken and wraps round to slot 0.

questions.onCorrect: A probe that runs off the end continues at slot 0, which is why the table is treated as a ring.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the slot 5 tries first, but 12 already holds it.
That slot is taken by 19, which probed there from slot 5.

questions.prompt: A hash table has 8 buckets and stores 12 entries. What is its load factor?
hints: Load factor is a ratio of two counts.
Divide the number of entries by the number of buckets.
Work out 12 ÷ 8.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 entries ÷ 8 buckets = 1.5.

questions.onCorrect: A load factor above 1 is possible with chaining, where a bucket can hold more than one key, and it means the chains are longer than one on average.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the buckets by the entries. The load factor is entries divided by buckets.

questions.prompt: The one-pass method runs on `[3, 2, 4]` with target 6, storing each number with its index after checking it. At which index j does the loop find the pair?
hints: At each x, check whether target − x is already stored, before storing x.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At index 0 the partner 3 is not stored, at index 1 the partner 4 is not stored, and at index 2 the partner 2 is stored, so the pair is found at j = 2, with indices 1 and 2.

questions.onCorrect: An element is never paired with itself, because it is stored only after its own check.

misconceptions.feedback: At index 1 the partner needed is 4, which has not been met yet. The pair is completed later.

questions.prompt: A hash table has 6 buckets and stores 15 entries. What is its load factor?
hints: Divide the number of entries by the number of buckets.

Work out 15 ÷ 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides buckets by entries. The load factor is entries divided by buckets.

questions.prompt: Linear probing in a table of 8 slots with hash k mod 8. Insert 5, 13, 21 and 6 in that order. In which slot does 6 end up?
hints: Work out each key's first slot. 5, 13 and 21 all leave remainder 5.

misconceptions.feedback: Slot 6 is its own slot, but 13 holds it by then.

questions.prompt: What is the name for two different keys that land in the same bucket?
hints: Two keys cannot both occupy the same place without a conflict.

questions.prompt: `fact(n)` returns 1 when `n` is 0, and `n * fact(n - 1)` otherwise. When `fact(5)` is running at its deepest point, how many calls are active at the same time?
hints: The first call is `fact(5)`, and each call makes a call with a smaller argument.
The chain stops when the argument reaches 0.
Count the calls with arguments 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The calls have arguments 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0, and all six are active when `fact(0)` runs.

questions.onCorrect: Every call in the chain is still waiting for the next one when the base case is reached, so the stack depth equals the number of calls in the chain.

misconceptions.feedback: That stops at `fact(1)`. The chain continues to `fact(0)`, which is also a call and also holds a frame.

questions.prompt: `fact(n)` returns 1 when `n` is 0, and `n * fact(n - 1)` otherwise. What does `fact(6)` return?
hints: The base case gives 1 for `fact(0)`, and each frame above it multiplies by its own `n`.

Multiply 6 by the value of `fact(5)`.
questions.onCorrect: Each return multiplies the value from the frame above by that frame's own n, so the answers build up from the base case.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6. The function multiplies n by the result of the smaller call.
That multiplies 6 by 5 only. The smaller call `fact(5)` returns 120, not 5.

questions.prompt: `flatten` is called on `[1, [2, [3, 4]], 5]`. Counting the first call, how many calls to `flatten` are made in total?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are three lists: the outer one, `[2, [3, 4]]` and `[3, 4]`, so `flatten` is called 3 times.

hints: Each list in the structure is flattened by exactly one call.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The lists are the outer list, `[1, 2]`, `[3, [4]]` and `[4]`, so there are 4 calls.

questions.onCorrect: The number of calls equals the number of lists in the nested structure.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the lists directly inside the outer one. One of them contains a further list, and that list is flattened by a call too.

questions.prompt: `fib(n)` returns `n` when `n` is less than 2, and `fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)` otherwise. Counting the first call, how many calls does `fib(4)` make in total?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `fib(4)` makes 1 call, `fib(3)` makes 5 calls, and `fib(2)` makes 3 calls, and 1 + 5 + 3 = 9.

questions.onCorrect: Each call with n of 2 or more adds two more calls, so the tree grows by branching and not in a single chain.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts a chain of calls, like fact. fib calls itself twice, so the calls branch.

questions.prompt: `fib(n)` returns `n` when `n` is less than 2, and `fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)` otherwise. Counting the first call, how many calls does `fib(6)` make?
hints: Use calls(n) = 1 + calls(n − 1) + calls(n − 2), with calls(0) = calls(1) = 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the first call itself. The recurrence adds 1 for it.

questions.prompt: Insertion sort is run on `[3, 6, 1, 5, 2, 4]`. How many shifts, moves of a larger item one place right, does it perform in total?

questions.prompt: Quicksort with the last item as pivot runs on an already sorted list of 10 distinct items. How many comparisons does partitioning make in total, over all the recursive calls?
